articles.title: Why Beijing wants us to go quiet
articles.summary: Last Tuesday, Secretary Tess Lazaro and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke by phone. Our DFA called the conversation frank, pragmatic and constructive. Both sides agreed to keep talking, manage…

blocks.text: Last Tuesday, Secretary Tess Lazaro and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke by phone. Our DFA called the conversation frank, pragmatic and constructive. Both sides agreed to keep talking, manage differences and avoid actions and rhetoric that could raise tensions before the Asean summit.
That sounds good. Nobody in the Philippine government is against keeping an open line of communication with China.
But I read the other side’s version, too, and I suggest every Filipino do the same.

In Xinhua’s account, Wang told Lazaro that relations are suffering from malicious interference by a small number of Filipino politicians who keep attacking China and crossing its red lines. He asked Manila to tighten its oversight of the individuals concerned and speak with one rational, unified voice on China.
He did not name anyone. He did not need to.

So let us not pretend this was only about lowering the temperature. Beijing just asked our government to muzzle its own people, specifically those who show the public what happens in the West Philippine Sea.
And now there are voices here saying perhaps we should oblige, perhaps transparency has done its job, perhaps it is time to be quiet for the sake of good relations.
Before we go down that road, we should ask a simple question: Why does China want us quiet, and who benefits if we are?
Why transparency bothers them
I have been part of this since the beginning, so let me explain what transparency actually did.

Before 2023, what happened at sea stayed at sea. The China Coast Guard would block us, ram us and hit us with water cannons, and the public would find out, if at all, through a diplomatic note filed weeks later. Beijing’s denial would come out the same afternoon.
Their story traveled. Ours did not.
We changed that.
We began releasing videos, photographs, the exact time and location of each incident, and the legal basis for Philippine presence and jurisdiction, usually within hours.
The water cannon attacks at Bajo de Masinloc. The military-grade laser pointed at our crew. The ramming of resupply boats at Ayungin. The swarming of vessels in our exclusive economic zone.
All of it is now on the record, documented not only by Filipinos who were there with us but also by independent foreign journalists who witnessed these incidents firsthand.
Yes, we deliberately leveraged one of our most cherished democratic values — freedom of the press — to help us tell the world the truth.
That is what Beijing cannot stand.

China can still deny what happened, but it must now contend with photographic and video evidence. In the past, Beijing could more easily control the narrative, using malign influence operations to shape domestic and international public opinion.
Our transparency initiative has fundamentally changed that dynamic, severely constraining China’s ability to manipulate information and distort the facts.
Anyone working in defense or foreign policy who fails to understand these dynamics and their implications for long-term Philippine interests is neglecting a fundamental responsibility.
First, they want the world to stop watching
Here is the first thing China gains if we go quiet: The world goes quiet with us.

When Washington, Tokyo, Canberra, Ottawa, Brussels or the G7 condemn the actions of the China Coast Guard in our waters, they are not reacting to our news conferences. They are reacting to the footage we release.

A foreign minister can issue a statement of concern based on compelling video evidence. No government issues such a statement based on rumors, much less on a confidential note verbale or diplomatic démarche delivered weeks after the incident.
The same footage helps sustain the security partnerships we have built.

Every like-minded government has to explain to its own parliament and people why it signs a maritime cooperation agreement with Manila, why its coast guard sails with ours and why it helps support our modernization.
The daily record of Chinese behavior in the West Philippine Sea is their justification.
Take it away, and supporting the Philippines becomes an abstraction. Abstractions do not survive a budget hearing.
Beijing knows this. I am not sure all of our own officials do.
When dealing with an actor that has lied many times and fooled us on numerous occasions, silence does not buy us greater diplomatic space.
It simply takes us back to how things were before 2023, when China kept pushing the envelope and we filed diplomatic protests whose full contents nobody ever saw.
Second, they are already thinking about 2028
The second thing is longer-term and more cynical.

China has learned from our last two elections that being seen as close to Beijing is now a liability in Philippine politics. Candidates who once proudly boasted of their friendship with China now prefer to change the subject.
Transparency is a major reason why.

It is difficult to campaign on the claim that China is our friend when voters can see, on their own phones, Chinese Coast Guard vessels firing water cannons at Philippine Coast Guard ships, threatening Filipino fishermen and depriving them of their livelihoods.
Beijing’s answer to that problem is not to change how it behaves at sea. It is to make sure nobody sees it anymore.
If transparency ends in 2027, the West Philippine Sea is out of the news by 2028. People forget.
The field is then wide open for politicians who owe Beijing, backed by Beijing’s money, to take back Malacañang and put the next president on a leash for six years.
That is what this is really about.
Not this year’s ASEAN summit. Not this month’s APEC.
It is about who sits in the Palace after 2028 and whether that person answers to the Filipino people or to someone else.
They cannot even agree on who called whom
One last detail from this week, because it tells you everything about who we are dealing with.
Our DFA says Secretary Lazaro received the call from Wang. Xinhua says Wang took the call at Lazaro’s request.
China’s malign influence operators got to work and reinforced this messaging to make the Philippines appear desperate.
The Chinese term they used, 应约, is the formula Beijing uses when the other side asked for the conversation.
In other words, the two governments cannot agree on who picked up the phone first.
And this is not the first time.
In December 2023, Beijing said then-Secretary Manalo had requested his call with Wang. Diplomatic sources in Manila insisted it was the Chinese side that called.
Twice now, on the most trivial of things in diplomacy, China has told the world a different story from the one it told us.
Both times, the story made the Philippines look like the one coming to Beijing, hat in hand, to patch things up.
And this latest one came barely two weeks after their ambassador reminded us that China could easily win if it chose to use force.
And now Beijing is asking us to trust its good faith and stop documenting what its ships do in our own waters.
Think about that.

If China is willing to rewrite the record of a phone call, what would stop it from doing the same with a water cannon attack, a ramming incident or the next confrontation at Bajo de Masinloc or Ayungin?
Without footage from our side, Beijing would be free to push its version of events, with little evidence available to challenge it.
That is precisely why transparency must continue.
Diplomacy with China remains necessary, but it must never come at the expense of documenting what happens in our waters.
Footage provides evidence that Beijing cannot simply dismiss or explain away.
A country that cannot be honest about who dialed cannot be trusted to be honest about anything that matters more.
[About the Author: Rear Admiral Jay Tristan Tarriela, Ph.D., is the Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea and commander of the West Philippine Sea Transparency Group.]
For comprehensive coverage, in-depth analysis, visit our special page for West Philippine Sea updates. Stay informed with articles, videos, and expert opinions.

articles.title: 5 dead in Malasiqui fireworks factory blast: What we know so far
articles.summary: The factory may have been operating illegally, according to local authorities. Neighbors thought the place was a piggery.

items: An explosion in Malasiqui, Philippines, killed five people, including three minors, and revealed a suspected illegal fireworks operation on a property previously known as a piggery.
Two survivors, an adult woman and a child, are in stable condition, while local officials are questioning the lack of permits for the operation and the legal status of the facility.
Authorities recovered materials used for manufacturing fireworks at the site, and plans are in place for police to monitor suspicious activities in the area following the incident.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MALASIQUI, Philippines – Five people, including three minors, were killed when an explosion ripped through a makeshift structure in Barangay Tabo-Sili here in Pangasinan on Wednesday night, November 4, exposing a suspected illegal fireworks operation on a property that residents believed was being used as a piggery.
The explosion, which occurred at around 7:45 pm, left two survivors: an adult woman and a child. Malasiqui police chief Police Lieutenant Colonel Francisco Sawadan said both were in stable condition.
The woman was the live-in partner of one of the fatalities, according to initial information about the victims.

The five fatalities included her male partner, a 17-year-old male, a female minor reportedly visiting the area, another male victim, and a 7-year-old girl who was rushed to a hospital but was later declared dead.

Beyond the loss of five lives, the incident has raised questions about how a suspected fireworks operation could have been established on a property in a remote barangay without the necessary government authorizations.
Residents said the explosion was powerful enough to be heard in neighboring barangays and nearby towns. Several more blasts followed in quick succession.
Barangay officials traced the source to a property near the boundary of barangays Tabo-Sili and Calbueg, although the site was within Tabo-Sili.
The Bureau of Fire Protection secured the area, preventing residents and local officials from approaching it that night because of safety concerns.
Malasiqui Vice Mayor Daria “Dang” Mamaril said she began receiving calls from residents reporting the explosion. She contacted the fire bureau and police, while the mayor proceeded to the scene.
The situation was distressing, she said, as victims were found scattered across the ground, some already lifeless.
Mamaril said no application for a fireworks factory or storage facility had ever been discussed before the Sangguniang Bayan.
Her statement raises questions about the legal status of the facility and whether the people operating it secured the necessary permits and clearances from other government agencies.
However, the absence of an application before the municipal council does not, by itself, establish whether other offices had received applications or issued relevant permits.
Authorities have yet to provide a complete account of the facility’s regulatory status.
“Talagang wala kaming idea (We really had no idea). I was also speaking with the barangay captain, wala rin silang alam (they also had no idea),” said Mamaril.
“We will make sure that a legislative action will be to call concerned agencies for investigation.”
Before the explosion, residents knew the property as a former piggery.
Barangay officials said the livestock operation had stopped several years ago after hogs reportedly died from an illness.

Tabo-Sili Barangay Captain Benjie de Vera said the property was previously operated by someone identified as only Lavarias, although the extent of Lavarias’ involvement in the property’s subsequent use has yet to be established.
After the piggery ceased operations, the property was eventually rented out again. The new occupants reportedly told residents they intended to resume raising pigs.
De Vera said local officials and residents had no reason to suspect that fireworks were being manufactured or stored there.
“Babuyan ito noon. Nagsimatayan yung mga baboy kaya hindi na inoperate ng may-ari. Pero may umupa ulit at sinabing magpapalaki uli ng baboy,” De Vera said.
(It used to be a piggery. The owner stopped operating after several pigs died. Someone later rented the property and said they would raise pigs again.)
De Vera said no one had reported suspicious visitors or unusual activities at the property before the explosion.
But the transition from a defunct livestock operation to a property where police would later recover firework materials remains an important part of the investigation.
Who rented the property after the piggery stopped operating? When did the new occupants move in? What activities were actually being conducted there?
These details have yet to be established publicly.
Barangay officials have yet to publicly explain whether any inspection or monitoring of the property took place after it was rented out again.
Initial police findings placed the explosion site around 600 to 700 meters from the nearest residential houses.
Two structures stood on the property: a former piggery and the makeshift structure where the explosion occurred.

During follow-up operations, the Pangasinan Police Provincial Office reported recovering raw materials suspected to be used in manufacturing fireworks, alongside finished products, including Baby Rocket fireworks and approximately 300 pieces of kwitis.
Police said their initial investigation indicated that the individuals occupying the property had no permit or authority to manufacture fireworks.

The Urdaneta City Forensic Unit processed the scene, with technical assistance from the provincial Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Canine Unit. Police Colonel Dennis de Leon, officer-in-charge and provincial director, also visited the area to oversee the response.

Authorities have yet to determine what triggered the explosion or conclusively establish whether the structure was being used to manufacture fireworks or merely store finished products and raw materials.

The blast also destroyed or damaged a pickup truck, a motorcycle, and a tricycle. Police described the pickup as a newly acquired, two-month-old, high-end vehicle. A final estimate of the damage has yet to be released.
Following the incident, the Malasiqui police station plans to issue an advisory to all 73 barangays through the Liga ng mga Barangay.
Sawadan said barangay officials would be urged to monitor new tenants, unfamiliar vehicles, and suspicious activities, particularly in isolated properties.
They were also asked to report businesses or activities that could pose a threat to public safety.
The planned advisory underscores the importance of closer coordination between barangay officials and police, especially when properties change ownership, tenancy, or business use.

The investigation has yet to establish who was operating the suspected fireworks facility, who owned or rented the property at the time of the explosion, and how long the operation had been running. – Rappler.com

articles.summary:
Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos arrested by secret service after telling officers voices told him to kill Donald Trump

blocks.text: The US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill Donald Trump.

The arrest Thursday night happened after secret service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. US officials said the suspect – Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican president.

Shortly after, officers discovered the suspect’s vehicle had been reported stolen and he had three firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition. This is the latest in a series of arrests the secret service and other law enforcement agencies have made against individuals who have threatened Trump or his family members’ lives since he returned to office last year.

The statement described Chrinos as an immigrant from Venezuela who is in the country illegally after entering the US through Texas in March 2024. DHS said he had been charged and was in US Marshals Service custody.
The White House did not provide comment, instead referring to DHS and the US secret service.

articles.title: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest
articles.summary: Ousted Paraguayan president Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied…

image.caption: Former paraguayan president Santiago Peña — seen here addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September — was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust. (Caitlin Ochs/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Ousted Paraguayan president Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.
Arrest ordered shortly after Senate removed him as president

In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies. The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, cutting nearly three million customers off from their savings and bank cards and setting off a political crisis.

Prosecutors ordered that Peña be held at his home until he can be brought before their economic crimes and anti-corruption unit, according to a letter to the national police commander. The attorney general's office confirmed to The Associated Press that he had been detained there. The order also called for the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, the former central bank chief Peña appointed. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo was in custody.

Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing.

Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. He inherits a government under pressure to return depositors' money and punish those behind Ueno's collapse.

A veteran of the long-ruling conservative Colorado party, Alliana, 52, is a former governor of the southern province of Ñeembucú and a former speaker of the lower house. He has not escaped the scandal entirely: Prosecutors are also investigating him, and on Thursday lawmakers shelved an opposition bid to impeach him.

Peña's removal also bars him from the lifetime Senate seat granted to elected former presidents under Paraguay's Constitution, denying him the parliamentary immunity that would accompany it. Prosecutors are also investigating current and former central bank and pension fund officials.
People protest against the government and Ueno Bank in Asunción, Paraguay, on Wednesday. (Jorge Saenz/The Associated Press)

Peña had submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it. His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that lawmakers should have approved his departure instead of pressing ahead with the impeachment trial.
In a farewell message released shortly before the verdict, Peña expressed hope his departure would spare Paraguay further harm.
"I do not want my presence to be a cause of greater division or instability," he wrote. "My responsibility is to put the country above my personal fate."
Growing public outrage

Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno's failure marched through downtown Asunción chanting, "Santi Peña to Tacumbú!" — a reference to the capital's main prison.
"This was an enormous betrayal of trust," said Yinal López, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno.

Ueno's implosion has plunged Paraguay into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade — and at dizzying speed. Regulators seized the bank before dawn Tuesday. By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado Party turned on him, led by former president Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña's longtime mentor. By Friday, his interior minister, chief of staff, legal adviser and political adviser had all quit.

It was a staggering reversal of fortunes for Peña, a telegenic technocrat and a former International Monetary Fund economist who owed his rapid political ascent to Cartes. The tobacco magnate, among Paraguay's richest men, made Peña his finance minister and twice backed him for president over rival factions' objections.
'Like a Shakespearean drama'

Once in office, though, Peña quietly amassed a rival power base, analysts say. Ueno Bank, flush with public deposits, became the centrepiece of both his business empire and his effort to win over provincial governors as he sought to escape Cartes' shadow.
"It's like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron," said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research centre. "But he did so on very fragile grounds."
Police stand guard outside of a closed Ueno Bank branch in Nemby, Paraguay, on Tuesday. (Cesar Olmedo/Reuters)

Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him demanded answers from the central bank about Ueno's lending, citing leaked internal reports that warned its loans to related companies put its solvency at risk. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña's leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protégé.
"Cartes put the nail in the coffin," said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. "Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry."
A view of the headquarters of Ueno Bank in Asunción, on Tuesday. (Jorge Saenz/The Associated Press)

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp: Prosecution had its chance but failed; VP begins defense Monday
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday hit back at the prosecution, saying the latter had its chance, but failed. It also said Duterte will begin her defense on Monday, November 9.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 8:02am
The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday hit back at the prosecution, saying the latter had its chance, but failed. It also said Duterte will begin her defense on Monday, November 9.
"The prosecution had its chance. It failed. On Monday, the Vice President begins her defense," Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for Duterte, said in a statement.

"We apparently live in two worlds. One where due process and fairness still reign—where an accused is not condemned before she is heard, and where allegations must be proven with clear and convincing evidence presented in court. The other is wherever Atty. Lorna Kapunan and her colleagues have decided these rules no longer apply," he added.

"One world seeks the truth. The other desperately tries to persuade an increasingly skeptical public with asinine sound bites built on half-truths and malicious speculation, spewed out in daily, obtrusive, and nauseating press briefings and interviews," Panelo said.
Duterte's spokesperson made the comments a day after private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said Duterte is the best evidence against herself.

Kapunan made the response when asked if the vice president taking the witness stand will enable her to answer the impeachable allegations, mainly amassing around P817 million worth of unexplained wealth.

“If the Vice President appears before the impeachment court, she will be the best evidence against herself due to her demeanor, the way she answers. Remember, when she was summoned in House [hearings], she refused to take an oath. Would she even take an oath to tell the truth and nothing but the truth?” Kapunan said.

“The only one she can blame is herself. She gave evidence against herself by declaring in her SALN interest in these companies,” Kapunan said, referring to declared assets of the vice president such as Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and GenCorp. Foods Industries Inc. which Duterte has not divested from even amid a constitutional prohibition.

Kapunan noted that the vice president’s statements of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALNs)—the same documents in which she did not declare cash on hand or in bank from 2019 to 2025, despite bank officials testifying that she had bank deposits—were signed by Duterte under oath.
"That is the situation of the VP. She is giving evidence against herself," she said.

Kapunan also said the P776 million in remittances sent to Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared banana chips company and an asset listed in the vice president’s husband's SALN, was another clear-cut indication of unexplained wealth, as the amount was not reflected in the Duterte couple’s joint SALN.
The defense team of Duterte has listed at least 24 initial witnesses it intends to present upon the resumption of the impeachment trial next week.
The impeachment trial of the vice president will resume on Monday, November 9, at 10 a.m. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Gov’t dismantling a grid monopoly is only half the job
articles.summary: A policy framework earns its worth only when physical power flows reliably across the wire

blocks.text: Dismantling the grid development monopoly is an overdue necessity to rescue stranded generation and break persistent transmission backlogs, but introducing alternative builders is not an automatic cure. Without rigorous engineering standards, transparent cost accounting, and genuine fixes for underlying right-of-way hurdles, replacing the builder merely shuffles administrative blame while leaving the grid vulnerable to prolonged disputes and consumer-borne costs.

A power plant can stand fully funded, mechanically commissioned, and ready to feed megawatts into the grid, yet remain completely stranded by a transmission line lagging months or years behind schedule.

For generation developers, every delayed circuit represents deferred revenue eroded by compounding debt service. For households and businesses, it means locked-in power that never arrives to exert competitive, downward pressure on soaring electricity tariffs. In the physics and economics of electricity, generation machinery is only as viable as the high-voltage corridor that carries its output to load centers.

This hard commercial reality underscores the government’s decision to dismantle the de facto monopoly on grid development by allowing qualified third parties—including generation companies and the National Transmission Corporation (TransCo)—to finance and construct designated transmission assets outside the sole auspices of the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP).

Opening an alternate runway for capital expenditure is an understandable response to endemic project bottlenecks. Yet whether this policy pivot delivers energization at a fair cost depends, not on bold policy pronouncements, but on mundane operational execution: project selection, technical alignment, cost recovery mechanisms, and verifiable accountability.

The reform has moved swiftly through the administrative machinery. The Department of Energy (DOE) laid the groundwork in January 2026 by authorizing generation-led transmission construction, followed in February by a policy framework designating priority projects for TransCo. The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) quickly codified these avenues under Resolution No. 18, Series of 2026, putting implementation rules into effect on July 1 and initiating formal consultations on implementation pacts among NGCP, TransCo, and private proponents.

While the regulatory calendar has progressed on paper, the definitive test of the policy lies strictly in the field. Investors and end-users gain nothing from theoretical declarations of authority unless they shorten critical-path construction schedules and bring lines into service. Regulatory and executive actions must ultimately be judged by how much reliable transmission capacity is energized and what consumers are charged to put it there. (READ: ​​Reliable power supply will support VisMin, PH’s economic momentum)

A clear legal foundation is non-negotiable. The Department of Justice (DOJ) issued an opinion validating the executive branch’s authority to introduce supplemental builders alongside the existing concession agreement.

However, that opinion came with a vital caveat: the DOJ had not reviewed the final language of three core implementing instruments. Because broad executive authority does not automatically insulate specific contractual mechanisms from judicial challenge, the final turnover agreements and inter-agency protocols must be crafted with watertight precision to prevent disruptive litigation down the road.

Equally vital is maintaining the boundary between construction and system operation. Authorizing an independent power producer or state vehicle to string conductors and erect steel towers does not delegate the intricate task of balancing the national grid. NGCP remains the designated system operator, responsible for system reliability, grid stability, and dispatch coordination.

blocks.caption: [READOUT] The race to deliver cheaper power

blocks.text: Under the ERC’s guidelines covering approval, construction, technical turnover, and rate recovery, the interfaces between external builders and the grid operator will determine whether a newly built line is integrated cleanly or languishes in jurisdictional limbo.

NGCP’s own cautionary position warrants balanced assessment. The transmission concessionaire has affirmed the urgency of timely network expansion while evaluating the new rules against the terms of its franchise and concession agreement. The engineering rationale is indisputable: a high-voltage network cannot function as a patchwork of disparate components.

All new lines, whoever builds them, must strictly comply with uniform grid codes, technical protection schemes, and synchronized commissioning protocols. Rushing transmission construction without disciplined adherence to system-wide engineering standards risks severe vulnerabilities across the wider network.

Moreover, substituting the builder does not automatically eliminate the obstacles that delayed lines in the first place. Protracted right-of-way acquisitions, lengthy local government permitting, agrarian disputes, and court-issued expropriation delays hamper state agencies and private developers alike.

Interventions must therefore be preceded by an unsparing diagnosis of each stalled link. Regulators must articulate precisely what caused the delay, who holds the remedy, and why an alternate arrangement can break the impasse where the concessionaire could not. Otherwise, the state merely shuffles administrative responsibility while leaving stubborn structural obstructions unaddressed.

The economic ledger demands even stricter oversight. When a generator finances a transmission extension, it advances upfront private capital that must be recovered through predictable, lawful commercial terms.

While the ERC has pledged to restrict reimbursement strictly to prudent and reasonable project costs, that promise must be backed by radical transparency. Ratepayers deserve complete clarity on allowable capital costs, debt carrying charges, and how the assets are folded into regulated wheeling rates.

Regulators must also establish an airtight audit trail to guarantee that electricity consumers are never billed twice for identical physical assets or network improvements. Every peso recovered through retail electric bills must link directly to an identifiable, verified, and audited capital asset. (READ: [Vantage Point] System loss: The electricity consumers pay for but never receive)

Clear cost-allocation formulas must also govern lines initially built by a single generator that eventually serves subsequent power plants, thereby preventing windfalls and commercial disputes among network users.

The DOE’s commitment to publish priority project lists and mandate quarterly progress tracking from TransCo provides a welcome foundation for accountability. Making schedules, expenditures, and revisions publicly visible ensures that, when projects falter, the public can pinpoint whether the delay lies with private contractors, concessionaires, or bureaucratic inaction within the government itself.

Opening the grid to new builders is a sensible structural step, but broadening the construction pool elevates the standard of accountability across the board. NGCP must justify its execution record, the government must prove its interventions accelerate energization, and the ERC must safeguard the public against inflated costs. A policy framework earns its worth only when physical power flows reliably across the wire. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Meet the Bugkalot in Nagtipunan, Quirino
articles.summary: A journey into Nagtipunan, Quirino shows how the Bugkalot people left their fierce headhunting past behind to become a community centered around faith and bayanihan

blocks.text: ARTISANS. Tourists can learn the basics of bead making from the Bugkalot bead creators themselves.
Marky Ramone Go/Rappler
A journey into Nagtipunan, Quirino shows how the Bugkalot people left their fierce headhunting past behind to become a community centered around faith and bayanihan

items: The true essence of travel lies in engaging with local communities and their cultural heritage, as highlighted by the Lakbay Likha program in Quirino and Nueva Vizcaya.
The Bugkalot indigenous peoples, through cultural demonstrations and workshops, showcase their traditions and the impact of Christianity on their practices, including the abandonment of headhunting.
Lakbay Likha aims to foster deeper connections between travelers and local artisans, promoting cultural learning and supporting community livelihoods through hands-on experiences.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

While travel often focuses on postcard landscapes, the true heart of a destination lies in the communities that have called it home for generations. Through the work of cultural bearers, these communities sustain the traditions, knowledge, and heritage passed down through the ages.

Recognizing that travel can be more than sightseeing, the Department of Tourism (DOT) Region II and the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Region II developed Lakbay Likha. This tourism circuit in Quirino and Nueva Vizcaya brings visitors closer to local artisans, their crafts, and their communities through workshops and creative hubs where travelers can purchase local products and learn traditional skills.

In Nagtipunan, Quirino, Lakbay Likha introduces visitors to the Bugkalot indigenous peoples — also referred to as the Egongot — offering a cultural insight that no well-shot landscape photograph can capture.

blocks.caption: Myra dela Cruz (right), also a Bugkalot, presents the traditional clothing of the community.

blocks.text: As community members demonstrated traditional dances and chants, Myra dela Cruz, a Bugkalot member who has researched her own heritage, explained how customs continue to shape modern life in Nagtipunan.
For the Bugkalot, cultural preservation is woven into daily survival and mutual support.
“Bayanihan (community spirit) remains important to us, especially during occasions such as panhik (traditional courtship), weddings, and funerals,” Dela Cruz explained.
This same spirit extends to seasonal hunting and fishing, where catches are divided among households so that other families can benefit.

Agriculture remains the primary livelihood for Bugkalot families in Nagtipunan. Many cultivate corn as a cash crop, while upland rice is grown primarily for household consumption. Families also raise livestock like pigs and chickens for income.
The introduction of Christianity brought significant changes to Bugkalot culture, most notably the abandonment of headhunting.
Dela Cruz emphasized the role of Christian missionaries, particularly the New Tribes Mission led by Filipino missionary Florentino Santos (fondly called Apun Tino), who arrived in the 1950s.
The transition did not happen overnight. In his own accounts, the late Apun Tino acknowledged that the last instances of headhunting occurred as recently as the 1990s.

This timeline aligns with anthropologist Shu-Yuan Yang’s 2011 study, “Headhunting, Christianity, and History among the Bugkalot (Ilongot) of Northern Luzon, Philippines,” which notes that headhunting persisted in isolated areas for decades after Christian conversion began.

“Christianity played a major role in changing practices that the community came to regard as bad,” Dela Cruz explained, noting the sacrifices of early missionaries. “But the good traditions and rituals remained.”

The transformation eventually became internally driven. Bugkalot converts actively spread their faith across Kabugkalotan (their ancestral homeland), with many becoming pastors and missionaries to other indigenous groups in the Philippines.
For Dela Cruz, keeping Bugkalot traditions alive begins at home, passed from parents to children.
Traditional dances, like the Tagëm, and customary attire are showcased during community gatherings, giving younger generations a firsthand look at their living heritage.

However, true preservation goes beyond performance. Deeper engagement regarding language, oral histories, and ancestral knowledge is vital as younger generations navigate changing lifestyles and beliefs.

This is also what the Lakbay Likha program hopes to bring into its tourism circuits: experiences that go beyond visiting places and buying souvenirs, by giving travelers opportunities to learn directly from local artisans and take part in the creative practices of the communities they visit.

blocks.caption: A Bugkalot artisan shows the colorful materials used to craft the intricate beadwork.

blocks.text: By supporting local SMEs, community-based artisans, and creators, the program aims to make these encounters part of the travel experience while creating opportunities for the people behind the crafts.

In Nagtipunan, cultural learning was paired with a bead-making tutorial led by Bugkalot women who demonstrated the craft themselves. Guests were also able to buy many of their creations such as intricate bead accessories like beaded necklaces, bracelets, and more.

blocks.caption: Some of the beadworks created by the members of the Bugkalot community.

blocks.text: A memorable highlight of the visit occurred just prior to departure when a community member explained that the Bugkalot have a specific chant for bidding goodbye. Instructing the visitors to walk away, she promised to sing as they left.
As the vehicles pulled away, she stood waving with a microphone in hand, sending them off with the traditional chant.

It served as a fitting conclusion to an itinerary centered on learning about a culture. The experience left visitors with a deeper appreciation for Bugkalot traditions, the people keeping them alive, and the important role that community encounters play in travel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: U.S. sanctions Canadian money-exchange businesses connected to Iranian regime, Ryan Wedding
articles.summary: The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head…

image.caption: 'Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,' Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement. (Nathan Howard/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada·New

The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
Companies in Canada gave sanctioned Iranian entities 'financial lifeline,' treasury says

The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.

"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.

items: Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada

blocks.text: The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.

In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada.
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:

items: Diverse ‌Trade ⁠Inc., doing business as Million Exchange in Ontario.
1380079 BC Limited, doing business as Amin Exchange in B.C.
Top PC Technician Inc., operating in Ontario.
NIA Nations Currency Ltd., based in B.C.
2397639 Ontario Ltd., doing business as Farah Exchange.
CCC Inc. in Ontario.
B Galaxy Inc., doing business as Cryptoyal from the same Ontario location as CCC Inc.
Darvish Exchange in Ontario.

blocks.text: The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.

In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.

items: Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran

blocks.text: In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January.
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.

Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. articles.title: Paraguay Senate dismisses President Santiago Pena over bank crisis
articles.summary: Paraguay’s Senate has ousted President Santiago Pena over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government. Millions of customers' accounts are frozen, with public pension and health care funds…

image.caption: Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties (FILE: 03/03/2025)Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's Senate on Friday impeached President Santiago Pena over a banking crisis that left millions of people unable to access their deposits.
Senators voted overwhelmingly to remove Pena for misconduct in office.
The move cleared the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to succeed him. He will serve the rest of the presidential term, which ends in August 2028.

Pena had already resigned on Thursday, but by impeaching and convicting him instead of accepting his resignation, senators stripped him of the lifetime Senate seat and immunity granted to former presidents, leaving him vulnerable to prosecution.
Following the Senate vote, prosecutors ordered the arrest of the ousted president alongside former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo as part of a criminal investigation.
Why did Pena face impeachment?
Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties.
The bank's accounts — also used to process pension payments — are frozen, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money. Ueno also held hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds.
Pena's resignation on Thursday followed the withdrawal of support by Congress President Basilio Nunez and ruling conservative Colorado Party leader Horacio Cartes.

Thirty-five opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents had submitted impeachment articles in the 80-seat Chamber of Deputies, accusing Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to Ueno.
Pena sold his shares in Ueno Holding, whose businesses include the bank, in April 2025. Lawmakers also cited two loans he received from Ueno as part of allegations of improper financial gain.

They alleged improper presidential interference in the Social Security Institute, known as IPS, and preferential treatment for Ueno. IPS manages pension and health care funds for most Paraguayan workers and held $355 million at the bank — about 9% of its investments, according to financial manager Gladys Vera.

The motion also questioned Pena's 2023 appointment of central bank chief Carvallo, who previously chaired Financiera Ueno. According to the document, the central bank approved the company's conversion into a bank just 83 days after his appointment.
What happened to Ueno Bank?
Ueno served about 2.94 million customers, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

As of last month, the bank said it held roughly $800 million in public-sector deposits — about a quarter of its total deposits — including money from the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

blocks.caption: People took the the streets of Asuncion on WednesdayImage: Jorge Saenz/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's central bank ordered a resolution or closure process Tuesday after finding that Ueno's solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum.
Ueno's app, card payments and transfers stopped working, while branches closed, leaving customers queuing outside unable to withdraw their savings.
Hundreds of employees of Ueno and other companies in its parent conglomerate protested outside the Labor Ministry Thursday, demanding unpaid wages and severance.
Retirees, depositors, students and workers had marched through Asuncion a day earlier, demanding Pena's impeachment and holding signs saying "Give us back our money."
What have authorities done?

Authorities detained eight senior executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud.
Lawyers for several detainees said they needed time to review the allegations before commenting.
Pena had sought to reassure customers in a video message Wednesday, pledging legislation "that will return to every saver what they are entitled to as quickly as possible."
The crisis also forced him to cancel his attendance at the Ibero-American summit in Madrid.
Pena, a conservative economist, took office in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Editor's Note: This piece, originally published on November 5, was updated on November 7 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: Kapunan: Defense’s ‘I don’t know’ alibi makes VP Duterte look ‘dumb’

articles.title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
articles.summary:
Primary school students bested 200,000 competitors across New South Wales to reach the Premier’s Spelling Bee finals in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales. The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition. Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

blocks.caption: The tension is palpable on stage at the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.
To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.
The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.
Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.
In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.
“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.

blocks.caption: Alesha Kahfandi missed ‘antepenultimate’ but is tied for runner-up. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: But the show must go on.
after newsletter promotion

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.
“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.
But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”
“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

blocks.caption: Maximilian Lumley wins second place in the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee in Penrith in Sydney’s west. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”
Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.
“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”
Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.
“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

articles.title: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay at start of South America tour
articles.summary: Pope Leo has arrived in Uruguay at the start of a 12-day trip through three South American nations. His trip, which is intense with a packed itinerary, comes just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.

image.caption: Uruguay's President Yamandu Orsi welcomed Pope Leo as he landed in Carrasco International Airport Image: Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay on Friday at the start of a grueling 12-day tour through three South American countries, just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff told reporters he was very happy to be in Uruguay, having flown a nearly 14-hour flight from Rome to get to Montevideo.
"I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward," he told reporters aboard the papal plane.
Leo hit the ground running on arrival, drawing huge crowds in Montevideo as he pulled into town in his open-sided popemobile.
The Vatican estimated 30,000 people had turned out to watch him go by and attend his first event in a country that is largely secular and where membership in the Church is declining.

"In an age ‌when ​differences can easily become a source of conflict, persevering ​in respect for the law, negotiation and the ⁠patient ​search for ​agreements is a service ​that Uruguay ‌can continue to offer its neighbors," ​Leo ⁠told crowds in Montevideo's main square.
Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance, was present there too.
Leo is then planning to visit the Casavalle neighborhood, which is notorious for its high rates of poverty and violence.
With starting in Uruguay, Leo marks the first papal visit to the country in nearly four decades, with Pope John Paul II having last visited in 1988.
What to know about Pope Leo's taxing itinerary
The pontiff will spend three days in Uruguay before heading on to Argentina on Sunday.
He then travels to Peru, where he spent half his priestly life, before he was elected pontiff last year. He became a naturalized Peruvian citizen in 2015.
Latin America is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, for whom the pope is their spiritual leader. However, fewer and fewer people on the continent identify as Catholic.
Enthusiasm around Leo's visit a surprise in Uruguay

Uruguay, the most secular Latin American country, was the first country in the world to legalize recreational marijuana use and has since legalized abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all against opposition from the Catholic Church.
However, the enthusiasm around Leo's visit has come as a bit of a surprise, with tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium selling out in just two days.

blocks.caption: The pope is expected to express opposition to some of the more liberal policies enacted in UruguayImage: Lucas Aguayo Araos/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: What will Pope Leo do in Argentina?
On Sunday, Leo will cross over to neighboring Argentina, the home of his papal predecessor Francis, who, however, disappointed his native compatriots by never returning home as pope.
At the beginning of Francis's papacy, some 71% of Argentinians identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2024, this had fallen to 58%.

blocks.caption: Leo will hope his visit makes up for the refusal by his predecessor to visit his home countryImage: Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo is set to meet with Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has come under criticism from the Catholic Church for his sweeping cuts that have hampered programs for the poor and needy.
He is also planning to meet with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives.
Pope Leo to return to Peru for last leg of trip
The final leg of the trip, on Wednesday, will see Leo return to Peru, where he lived and preached for two decades.
There is excitement about his visit to Peru, with the pope planning to celebrate Mass in his old diocese of Chiclayo as well as in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
The pope will also celebrate Mass in the former Incan capital city of Cusco before honoring Peru's indigenous population by traveling to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon.
The excitement can be seen in the street vendors selling T-shirts and rosaries with his likeness, while bakeries have been selling Leo bread.
Peru has also seen a weakening of the faithful in recent years, with the Catholic population falling from 76% in 2013-2014 to around 67% now.

blocks.caption: Peruvian Catholics have shown particular interest in the pope's visit as a type of homecomingImage: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: Susie Wiles exits White House as Trump ousts another woman from key role
articles.summary: Wiles thanks president for ‘honor of a lifetime’ as departure leaves behind overwhelmingly male leadership team

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Friday said Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will leave her post, a major shake-up of his inner circle that comes amid a steady exodus of senior female officials from his administration.

The president announced her ouster – and her replacement, by the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller – in a post on Truth Social, days after a sweeping blue wave gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Wiles’s departure leaves behind an overwhelmingly male leadership team.
“I wanted to make a change,” he told reporters on Friday. “I think Susie’s done a very good job … Stephen’s been great and we’ve got to make moves.”

Wiles, who reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night, said her role as chief of staff “has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America first.”

Wiles’s exit follows a string of high-profile resignations and dismissals of women in the Trump administration. In recent months, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted just five days after taking up the role, while former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem and former attorney general Pam Bondi were also dismissed.
Former national intelligence director Tulsi Gabbard reportedly resigned under pressure, while Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former US ambassador to Greece, has also departed her post.

As high-ranking women left the administration, Wiles, diagnosed with breast cancer, stayed put, with Trump even claiming at one point: “She’s going to be here for a long time”. Wiles announced in September that she was cancer-free.

Just a day before Trump’s announcement of Wiles’s ouster, Harmeet Dhillon, a staunch Trump ally and controversial head of the justice department’s civil rights division, also resigned, marking yet another high-profile woman’s departure from the Trump administration.

Dhillon’s resignation comes amid expectations Democrats will use their majority in Congress to investigate federal agencies under Trump, including the US justice department, which has repeatedly been accused of being weaponized by the administration to pursue Trump’s own political enemies.

Other justice department officials have also since resigned amid the major post-midterm personnel shakeup, including John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security, as well as Jason Reding Quiñones, a key attorney that led inquiries into Trump’s rivals.
Only a handful of women remain in Trump’s cabinet, including agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins and Kelly Loeffler, head of the Small Business Administration.

Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old political aide, remains a frequent presence by the president’s side at public events. Harp has previously written letters to the president in which she described him as “my guardian and protector”.

articles.title: DNA profile created for grizzly behind deadly attack in B.C.
articles.summary: The investigation into a suspected fatal grizzly attack this week includes DNA profiling to identify the animal responsible.

image.caption: Hundreds of grizzlies are estimated to live in the region around Bella Coola, B.C., according to government estimates. (Amir Said/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The investigation into a suspected fatal grizzly attack this week includes DNA profiling to identify the animal responsible.
Forensics expert says finding a killer bear is very similar to using DNA from crime scenes to find suspects

B.C. Conservation Officer Service Insp. Jeff Tyre said this week that his team is creating a DNA profile of the bear using materials left at the scene where a mother and daughter were found dead on a trail just outside of Bella Coola on B.C.'s Central Coast.
That profile will be cross-referenced with DNA collected from any bears they manage to trap and if it is a match, the bear will be killed, he said.

Forensics expert Dean Hildebrand — founder of the B.C. Institute of Technology Forensics DNA Lab, which is not involved in the investigation — said the use of DNA for an investigation is "very similar to what we do in humans."

items: Mother and daughter killed in suspected grizzly attack were 'two peas in a pod,' family says
More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: Hildebrand said only trace amounts of DNA would be needed to create the profile, which can then be held indefinitely as an electronic file to check against any future attacks.

"We have a crime scene index in Canada where we get DNA profiles from crime scenes unsolved. They go into a database and they just sit there and those things can link crime scenes together until the other side comes together where you get the offender. So it would be exactly analogous to this."
LISTEN | How DNA is used to track grizzlies after an attack:
Daybreak North5:34Using DNA to find a deadly grizzly bear
DNA profile also created in 2025 attack

Tyre confirmed they would also check the sample from this week's attack against the DNA profile created for the grizzly behind a November 2025 incident where a group of students and teachers were injured by a bear in Bella Coola.
Though eight bears were trapped and released in the aftermath of that case, the bear was never found. No bears have been trapped following this week's attack, he said.

The search continues for a grizzly bear believed responsible for a deadly attack on a mother and daughter near Bella Coola, B.C., this week. Members of the public are urged to avoid the Snooka West Trail area. (B.C. Conservation Officer Service)
But he also said DNA testing is a crucial element of the investigation because there are "so many bears" in the area, making it difficult to count.
Bella Coola, about 400 kilometres northwest of Vancouver as the crow flies, is part of the Great Bear Rainforest, a region protected in part because of its importance to grizzly bears.
Coastal First Nations, including the Nuxalk Nation whose territory encompasses Bella Coola, have long coexisted with the animals that are a crucial part of their culture.

items: Suggested curfew, night patrols in place following suspected fatal grizzly attack near Bella Coola
Call to renew licensed grizzly bear hunting met with pushback from B.C. conservationists

blocks.text: "Nuxalk have lived with bears for thousands of years, and we consider them to be our kin," Elected Chief Samuel Schooner said in an emailed statement this week. Schooner said his community is taking time to heal from this week's attack, which has reopened trauma from last year, but emphasized that any decisions about how to live with bears moving forward will come from within.

In the meantime, Nuxalk leadership is working with conservation officers and RCMP to provide support and protection, which includes providing escorts for children going to school and offering rides to anyone who needs to get around.
With files from Daybreak North

articles.title: 4 reasons to watch Canada in the women's hockey world championship
articles.summary: Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship

image.caption: Canada's players celebrate their first goal goal score by Jessie Eldridge (9) during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship
Canada has shaken up the team at every level after some heartbreaking losses

Yes, there's the patriotism of cheering for your country, and yes, there's the Canada/U.S. rivalry, but those aren't the only reasons to watch Team Canada in the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship.
Canada dominated Sweden 5-1 in its world women's hockey championship opener Friday to kick off the 11-day, 10-nation tournament in Denmark. Their next game is Sunday, when they face Japan.
The U.S. and Canada are the tournament favourites, continuing a long-standing cross-border rivalry. Canada has won 13 world titles followed by the U.S. with 11 spanning the previous 24 championships.
But this year, there are even more reasons it's worth paying attention to the Canadian team. Here are a few of them:
Jesse Eldridge leads Canada past Sweden at the worlds
1. The youngest lineup in decades
To quote Hockey Canada's Women's Worlds preview, "the kids have arrived."

The average age of this roster is 26 years, two months and 22 days — the youngest roster Canada has played at the Women’s Worlds since 2013, Hockey Canada notes. Three of the youngest players are debuting in Denmark: Rosalie Tremblay (age 18), Hayley McDonald (age 18), and Sara Manness (age 19).

items: 7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: Three other collegiate players, 19-year-old Chloe Primerano (University of Minnesota), 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer (University of Minnesota Duluth) and 23-year-old Ève Gascon (University of Minnesota Duluth) return for their second world championship.
The oldest player is goaltender Ann-Renée Desbien, who is 32.

Canada's goalkeeper Ann-Renée Desbien makes a save during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark on Friday. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)
2. Poulin is out
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin has been sidelined due to knee surgery after tearing her ACL last spring, leaving the Canadian team without its captain for the first time in more than a decade.

Poulin is widely regarded as one of the greatest women's hockey players of all time. She's won three Olympic gold medals, scoring the winning goal in all three of those gold-medal games to earn the nickname "Captain Clutch."

items: What to know for the women's hockey world championship
7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: A five-time Olympian, Poulin is also the all-time leading goal scorer for the Canadian women's team at the Winter Games with 20. With her out, Canada is playing in its first international tournament without Poulin on the roster since she made her national team debut in 2009.
Defender Renata Fast and forward Laura Stacey are sharing Canada's captaincy in Denmark.
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin provides update about her health
3. New head coach and management
The Canadians ended last season with a heartbreaking loss in the Olympic gold-medal game against the Americans. Since then, there's been change at all levels for Canada.

The group has new leadership, starting with Hockey Hall of Famer Danièle Sauvageau, who returns to the Hockey Canada fold as GM of the senior national team. Ottawa Charge GM Mike Hirshfeld and PWHL Detroit GM Manon Rhéaume are serving as assistant GMs.

items: Mix of young, veteran players invited to Canadian women's hockey team camp

blocks.text: There's also a new head coach: Kori Cheverie, who led Sauvageau's Victoire to a Walter Cup in the spring. Cheverie has been an assistant with the national team since before the 2022 Olympic gold-medal win.

Montreal Victoire head coach Kori Cheverie hoists the Walter Cup alongside general manager Daniele Sauvageau during the Montreal Victoire's victory celebration in Montreal in May. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
4. Coming off some big losses

The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 worlds and claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and the Olympic gold medal at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.
Canada was also swept in the Canada/U.S. Rivalry Series that concluded last December. So now, with a fresh roster and without its greatest star, Canada is looking to reclaim the championship.

The final is set for Nov. 16. While it's not necessarily guaranteed that Team Canada will make it, it's been Canada vs. the U.S. in 23 out of the last 24 finals. The lone exception came in 2019, when host Finland shocked the Canadians in the semis before losing a controversial final against the States.
With files from CBC's Karissa Donkin and Jesse Campigotto, Reuters and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Canada's foreign minister urges G7 to turn up heat on Putin after deadly Ukraine strike
articles.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is pressing G7 allies to intensify pressure on Russia after an attack on a Ukrainian aid distribution site killed 53 people. Anand says the international…

image.caption: A rescuer uses a drone detector during a search operation at the site of an underground shelter that was used as a humanitarian aid hub in Russia's Zaporizhzhia region. The hub was hit by a Russian airstrike on Monday. (Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is pressing G7 allies to intensify pressure on Russia after an attack on a Ukrainian aid distribution site killed 53 people. Anand says the international community must strengthen sanctions and military support, and confront Moscow directly when world leaders gather for December's G20 summit in Florida.
Anand demands stronger collective action as Russian attacks intensify

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says she'll make a point of pushing her G7 colleagues to take further, concerted action against Russia following this week's horrific strike on an aid distribution site in Ukraine.

Anand will be meeting with her counterparts this weekend in Paris and said Friday that the issue of Moscow's unrelenting campaign targeting civilians should also be a topic of conversation at the G20 later this year near Miami.

The death toll from Russia's bombing earlier this week of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region rose on Friday to 53, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure caused renewed power outages in seven Ukrainian regions, the country's deputy energy minister said.

items: Ukraine's winter warning to Canada: Help us keep the lights on

blocks.text: Anand said the strikes, which came as U.S. First Lady Melania Trump tried to further mediation efforts, "necessitates collective action over and above what we are putting on the table" in terms of sanctions and economic and military support.
"I will be raising the need for collective effort with my G7 counterparts," Anand said following a meeting in Ottawa with her Austrian counterpart.

U.S. President Donald Trump has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the mid-December gathering of G20 world leaders at his Doral, Fla., golf club. Putin has not yet decided whether he will accept the invitation.
Anand said the world community shouldn't waste the opportunity to confront Russia.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with Austrian Foreign Affairs Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger on Friday in Ottawa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

"At the G20 in December, this issue must be raised amongst countries at the table, especially given that Russia will be represented there and it will be an opportunity to speak directly to them," Anand said.
At a recent meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, in preparation for the upcoming summit, Anand confronted Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

She said she sat directly across the table from Lavrov, looked him straight in the eye and condemned Russia's "horrific crimes" and full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Anand and some European ministers refused to participate in the routine "family photo" because she didn't want to be pictured alongside Lavrov.

items: Death toll from Russian attack in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region climbs to 53

blocks.text: Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said she is particularly worried about the recent strikes in Zaporizhzhia because the region hosts Ukraine's largest nuclear power complex, which has been under Russia occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion.
She said she's in favour of further tightening international pressure on the Kremlin.
"There's one person only to decide to stop the war and it would stop immediately. This is Vladimir Putin," Meinl-Reisinger said.
"He is not able to win this war militarily. So we have to continue to put pressure that he is ready to negotiate for real this time."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
