articles.title: 'My final years poisoned': Court hears 90-year-old rape victim's powerful statement written before her death
articles.summary: A dangerous offender and sentencing hearing is underway in Calgary for Duran Ross Buffalo, 41, who was convicted of aggravated sexual assault and break-and-enter to commit sexual assault by a jury…

image.caption: A 90-year-old woman who was the victim of a rape in 2021 wrote a victim impact statement before she died in 2024. That statement was read at the sentencing hearing for her rapist, Duran Ross Buffalo. (David Mercer/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

A dangerous offender and sentencing hearing is underway in Calgary for Duran Ross Buffalo, 41, who was convicted of aggravated sexual assault and break-and-enter to commit sexual assault by a jury last year.
Duran Ross Buffalo, 41, facing dangerous offender designation
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

After 90-year-old Mary was raped, she got herself to a hospital, only to be “turned away with a pat on the head,” her son told a courtroom as he read aloud his victim impact statement at a hearing for the man who violently attacked his mother.
Mary is not the victim’s real name; it is a pseudonym CBC News has used in order to respect a publication ban protecting her identity.
Prosecutors are trying to have Buffalo designated as a dangerous offender and handed an indeterminate sentence.

items: 'I can't stop crying': Jurors hear tearful 911 call from 90-year-old rape victim

blocks.text: Before she died in 2024, Mary learned that her rapist had been caught and charged, and she wrote a powerful victim impact statement that was read aloud by her daughter on Friday morning.
'The rape is now a part of me'
The assault, said Mary, “ruined the life that day; destroyed it.”
“The rape is now part of my person, an ugly part.”

For more than a decade before the assault, Mary had been living in a secure assisted living apartment building in Calgary where residents would leave their doors ajar so that home care workers could let themselves in.
On Jan. 1, 2021, Buffalo broke into the apartment building and staff called police. Officers searched the building for about 20 minutes before assuming he had left.
'He was too strong for me'
In reality, Buffalo was hiding in the storage room of Mary's apartment.
“I was awakened later sensing someone in my room and opened my eyes to see this man at the end of my bed,” wrote Mary. “I tried desperately to fight him, but he was too strong for me.”
Mary said she weighed less than 100 pounds at the time and was under five feet tall.
She described Buffalo holding her down with his hand over her mouth to muffle her screams.
“When it was over, I could hardly believe I was alive,” she said.
Home alone in a taxi
Mary got herself to a hospital, where she said medical staff believed her early-stage dementia was to blame for her story.
Around 5 a.m., hours after being raped, Mary took a taxi back to her apartment.
She wrote that she was “distraught, and not believed. It was an awful experience. I felt so helpless.”
Her daughter arrived from Edmonton that morning and discovered Buffalo’s shirt in her mother’s apartment. They called police, and officers took Mary for a rape kit at a nearby urgent care centre.
'He stole my peace of mind'
“I agreed to do this because I wanted people to understand this assault really happened to me,” she wrote.
In the aftermath, Mary said she felt “traumatized, cold, violated and scared that this could happen again to me.”
She ended up leaving Calgary, where her husband is buried, so that she could live with her daughter in Edmonton.
“This man stole my home from me; he stole my peace of mind,” said Mary. “To have my final years poisoned … left me sad and weary and lonesome.”
'Still bruised'
Buffalo’s dangerous offender hearing continues next week.
Court of King’s Bench Justice Michele Hollins has already heard evidence presented by prosecutors Matt Dalidowicz and Stephanie Morton that Buffalo is in the highest risk category for reoffending.

items: Dangerous offender hearing underway in Calgary for man who raped 90-year-old, sexually assaulted 5 kids

blocks.text: He has a 20-year history of sexual and violent offences, including crimes against children as young as four years old. Prosecutors say Buffalo’s risk to the community is unmanageable.
After his attack on Mary, her “health spiralled downhill immediately,” according to her son.
She died in 2024.
Before her death, Mary wrote that she was no longer able to look at herself in the mirror.
“The outside bruises have now faded, but I am still bruised emotionally.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
articles.summary:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments

Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly…

blocks.text: Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.

According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.

With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money.

The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. The men allegedly stole nearly $5m from a hospital system headquartered in Missouri; about $2.7m from a Rhode Island bank, about $3m from a California hospital system, over $4.6m from a mutual fund headquartered in Massachusetts and about $5m from a pet food company in Florida. The men also stole over $11m from a UK tech company.

The men would direct employees to wire money to bank accounts all over the world including in the United States, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. After the money had been wired, the men would covert the money into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distributed it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators”, according to the DoJ press release. Soall and Hazan went by several aliases: Soal’s nicknames included “Seba Clarke” and “Rocky Balboa,” while Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Fat Boy,” and “Ron.”
In a statement, Jamie McDonald, a US attorney, said artificial intelligence had great potential but that the public should recognize that some may seek to use the technology to pursue criminal goals.

“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large-scale fraud,” said James C Barnacle Jr, the FBI assistant director in charge, in a statement. “As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”
The men have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, various counts of money-laundering conspiracy and aggravated identity theft.

articles.title: Restaurant owner defends planned ban on children under 15 amid backlash
articles.summary: The chef and owner of a Jamaican restaurant set to open in Winnipeg's West End at the end of this month is facing both backlash and support for her decision to exclude some children from its dine-in…

image.caption: The owner of Miss Christine's Kitchen on Ellice Avenue, expected to open this month, plans to only serve people age 15 and older. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

The chef and owner of a Jamaican restaurant set to open in Winnipeg's West End at the end of this month is facing both backlash and support for her decision to exclude some children from its dine-in experience.
Lawyer says case for discrimination depends on circumstances, negative outcomes experienced by complainant
Christine Pattison recently posted on social media that she plans to only allow people age 15 and older at Miss Christine's Kitchen on Ellice Avenue.
Pattison received swift criticism, she said in an interview on Information Radio with guest host Cory Funk on Friday.
She said she has been accused of breaking the law and discriminating against children.
Pattison's goal is to create a quiet and intimate experience that would be disrupted or ruined by kids running around and screaming, she said.
"Personally, I think it's a great idea," said Pattison, who has seven grandchildren, age four to 21.
"I want to give [customers] a space where they can come without their kids and have a wonderful evening, because it's so cozy and nice in there."
Christine Pattison, the chef and owner of Miss Christine's Kitchen, says some parents don't adequately control their children, making dining at restaurants less enjoyable. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)
Guests will be welcomed on a reservation basis, and the restaurant won't have a kids' menu, high chairs or a changing table.
"If anyone says that their kids never drive them crazy, they are a big fat liar."
Pattison decided to go this direction because of bad experiences at her previous restaurant, where children were permitted.
"That's all fine, but for this space, I wanted to create something special for adults only," she said.

Pattison feels her decision was somewhat validated after a visit by two of her grandchildren, age four and six. They left taps on in the washroom, played with burning candles and ran around dragging things, she said.
Pattison isn't surprised by the backlash but said many people have emailed her messages of support.
Legality 'depends': lawyer
One attorney who practises human rights law said businesses must comply with Manitoba's human rights code, which includes not discriminating based on age and family status.

While the code doesn't establish a test for proving discrimination, case law does, said Joëlle Pastora Sala, who works with the Public Interest Law Centre in Winnipeg, in conversation with host Marjorie Dowhos on Radio Noon.

Pastora Sala said she is not involved in the case at Miss Christine's Kitchen and her comments are not legal advice, but an often-cited legal decision in British Columbia said to prove discrimination, complainants have to show they suffered adverse impacts from a policy.
"Once you've done that, then the establishment — or the restaurant, in this case — would have to justify … the alleged discrimination," Pastora Sala said.
Joëlle Pastora Sala, a lawyer with the Public Interest Law Centre, say generally speaking, determining illegal discrimination depends on a number of factors. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)
In other words, the restaurant would have to justify that the age they identified is rationally connected to the service, she said.
Pastora Sala could not speak to whether Pattison's reasons were "justifiable enough."
"The classic … answer would be that it depends," she said.
It would depend on the age identified, the circumstances and the negative outcomes that a complainant suffered, Pastora Sala said.
If businesses are found to have violated human rights, the courts may offer various remedies, including financial compensation.

items: Years-long waits for human rights complaint hearings in Manitoba point to 'broken' system, lawyer says

blocks.text: Businesses may also be directed to change policies and undergo training.

Pattison said she has called the Manitoba Human Rights Commission to see if her plan violates human rights, but she didn't immediately connect with anyone. She expects a response within five to 10 days.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rosanna Hempel is a multiplatform journalist with a background in biology and forestry. She has been with CBC Manitoba since 2023, covering everything from extreme weather, health and housing to issues affecting Indigenous communities. She previously worked at CJOB/Global Winnipeg, where she was part of a team recognized by the Radio Television Digital News Association for its coverage of the 2023 Carberry bus crash. She speaks French and German. You can email her at rosanna.hempel@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Macklemore names US arenas he says refused to host 'Free Palestine' tour
articles.summary: Macklemore says after weeks of reaching out to U.S. venues, nine major arenas have refused to host his "Free Palestine" tour.

image.caption: US rapper Benjamin Haggerty, known as Macklemore, says after weeks of reaching out, nine U.S. arenas have refused to host his 'Free Palestine' tour. (Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Macklemore says after weeks of reaching out to U.S. venues, nine major arenas have refused to host his "Free Palestine" tour.
Madison Square Garden tells CBC News: 'he's not an arena level act'
Macklemore says that after weeks of reaching out to U.S. venues, nine major arenas have refused to host his "Free Palestine" tour.

The tour was launched after the Seattle-based rapper was removed as opening act for the U.S. leg of Ed Sheeran's tour after venues objected to his presence over his "Free Palestine" comments, with some accusing him of antisemitism and hate speech.
Sheeran's supporting acts stood in solidarity with Macklemore and also quit the Loop tour.
At the height of the controversy, Macklemore announced a three-date European tour, with all proceeds going to organizations supporting Palestinians.

The rapper said it was always his intention to bring the tour to the United States, but in an Instagram post Friday, he detailed some of the difficulties he has faced booking venues and called out nine specific arenas by name:

items: Madison Square Garden in New York
Prudential Center in Newark, N.J.
Barclays Center in Brooklyn
UBS Arena in Elmont, N.Y.
Intuit Dome in Inglewood, California
Kia Forum in Inglewood, Calif.
Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles
Chase Center in San Francisco
Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle

blocks.text: He said that by mid-September, he had a list of available dates at those arenas, but once the venues became aware he was inquiring for his Free Palestine tour, "those dates were suddenly off the table."
"In over twenty years of touring, I've never experienced anything like this," Macklemore said on Instagram.
CBC News has reached out to all of the arenas for comment.
An MSG Entertainment spokesperson told CBC News, "We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act."
Macklemore hats were on sale outside the Macklemore & Friends 'Free Palestine' Tour at The 3Arena in Dublin, Ireland in October. (Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)
Macklemore ended his lengthy post by promising more benefits for Palestine, even if he has to play outside.
"We will build our own stages. They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave
articles.summary:
Tech industry fears delays to its multi-trillion dollar infrastructure buildout meant to power artificial intelligence

Several newly elected Democrats and Senator Bernie Sanders have…

blocks.text: Several newly elected Democrats and Senator Bernie Sanders have renewed calls for datacenter moratoriums in the days after the US midterm elections. The sweeping Democratic victory, which was buoyed in part by backlash to the tech industry, has added momentum to efforts to slow down the multi-trillion-dollar buildout of the controversial facilities.

On the social media platform X, Sanders posted a call for an immediate national datacenter moratorium this week. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future,” Sanders said on Wednesday.
Sanders was joined by several Democrats, including Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona – a state where Elon Musk’s SpaceX has proposed a datacenter project that would span more than 700 acres.

“Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” Ansari posted Wednesday on X. Musk mocked her post in a retweet, and the two sparred, with Ansari forecasting congressional hearings, telling the centi-billionaire: “See you soon.”

The pushback to the buildout of datacenters, which tech companies need to power the AI products that have become central to their businesses, was one of the most visible issues of the midterms. Opposition to datacenters figured heavily in campaigns across the US, while voters passed dozens of local ballot measures aimed at restricting datacenter projects in their states.

The outcome of the midterm elections has so far alarmed tech investors and executives, with Meta platforms president Dina Powell McCormick telling the Wall Street Journal that it is “going to be harder” to build datacenters following the vote. After Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates and attacking Democrats on his social media platform, he jokingly posted on election night that “datacenters in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Post-midterms anxiety also helped fuel a massive selloff of AI stocks this week, as tech investors worried about new regulation such as datacenter pauses. White House National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett was confident that the construction of datacenters would continue, however, arguing to CNBC that the ballot initiatives largely wouldn’t affect existing projects.

Datacenters and AI opposition featured in numerous Democratic victory speeches after midterms, as newly elected representatives vowed to curb the power of Big Tech. In New Hampshire, Senator-elect Chris Pappas praised his constituents for “opposing big data centers that harm our communities”. New Mexico congressman Gabe Vasquez meanwhile proclaimed “the time is now to stop the AI billionaire class from forcing datacenters in our community.”
Several victorious Democratic candidates also promised that they would hand local communities the decision-making power over AI and data centers.
after newsletter promotion
“I do not work for data centers,” Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said to applause. “I work for you. I work for Ohio.”

Newly elected governors in several states key to the datacenter buildout, including Texas and Georgia, have also called for moratoriums on datacenters. Incoming Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa, whose state has become a hotspot for datacenter construction, pledged to halt new datacenter projects until new protections are in place.

“There are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of,” Hinojosa said this week on CNN. “We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections.”

articles.title: Cornell faculty declares ‘no confidence’ in school leaders in fallout from alleged gang-rape
articles.summary:
Faculty senate passed resolution expressing deep discontent with school’s response to alleged fraternity rape

Cornell University’s faculty senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring…

blocks.text: Cornell University’s faculty senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school’s top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student’s lawsuit saying she was gang-raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to members of the faculty senate on Friday afternoon.

The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and whether they’ve done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.

While the faculty body has no power over the university’s top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell’s trustees to urgently address what they viewed as longstanding institutional failures.
Voting took place electronically over more than a week, with the results released on Friday.

The Cornell community has been in a state of distress and dismay since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.

All of those men have denied her allegations, saying that either the sex was consensual or they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter, and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.

Cornell disciplined several of the accused students after a months long Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by the New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a taskforce to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have been furious with Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school’s disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

articles.title: This hawk gobbled up neighbourhood chickens until she got too fat to fly
articles.summary: When someone brought an immobilized red-shouldered hawk to the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center last month, staff suspected she was either blinded, injured or poisoned. But it turns out she just…

image.caption: This red-shouldered hawk was found immobilized in a driveway after eating too many neighbourhood chickens. She's now recovering at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center. (Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke/Facebook)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

When someone brought an immobilized red-shouldered hawk to the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center last month, staff suspected she was either blinded, injured or poisoned. But it turns out she just ate too many chickens.
'She's our big lady,' says director of Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center
When someone brought an immobilized red-shouldered hawk to the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center last month, staff suspected she was either blinded, injured or poisoned.
After all, the agile huntress should have been soaring through the sky and hunting unwitting prey. But instead, she was found belly-up in a driveway near Roanoke, Va.
After a series of X-rays and bloodwork, veterinary staff ruled out any injuries or health issues behind the creature's mobility issues.
Instead, they found she was 910 grams — almost twice the average weight for her species.
"[The] hawk's diagnosis was just that she's fat," Katherine McGrath, the wildlife rescue's director of operations, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "She's our big lady."
LISTEN | Interview with wildlife rescuer Katherine McGrath:
As It Happens6:03Hawk gobbles up neighbourhood chickens until she's too fat to fly
Filled with fowl
Once they had their diagnosis in hand, staff set about solving the mystery of how the hawk had gotten so hefty.

"Wild animals, unless they're being fed, typically do not get to a stage where we can clinically say that they're obese. So we thought someone was keeping her illegally as a pet, you know, or as a falconry bird," McGrath said.

The immobilized hawk weighed 0.91 kilograms, which is 910 grams or roughly one pound. Member of her species usually range from 500 to 700 grams, says the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center. (Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center/Facebook)
They reached out to the people who found her, but they weren't aware of anyone in the neighbourhood who practiced falconry or kept wild birds.
"And then we asked, 'Do any of your neighbours have free-roaming poultry or chickens or anything like that?" she said.
The finders chatted with their neighbours and learned that, yes, several of them kept free-roaming chickens, which had been inexplicably disappearing in recent weeks.
"And we were like, 'Ah, well, we have the bandit,'" McGrath said.
'She's healthy and angry'
McGrath says it's actually not that unusual for a hawk to eat so much it can't move.
Even a regular-weight hawk, she says, can become temporarily grounded after eating a large meal because the "balance of how much it takes for them to fly is so delicate."
What's more, she says, a hawk has no way of knowing when it's had enough. So an all-you-can-eat buffet of easy pickin' prey can be a recipe for disaster.
"Most wild animals, because they have to live through winter or live through lean times, if they have a good steady supply of food, they are going to … gorge themselves," McGrath said.
Staff at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center says this over-stuffed hawk will be ready to fly free in a matter of weeks. (Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center/Facebook)
But, all things considered, McGrath says their pudgy patient is doing just fine.
"She's actually showing all of the normal red-shouldered hawk behaviours," she said.
And by normal hawk behaviours, McGrath means she's wary of her human caretakers and mad as hell about her unwilling captivity.
"She does what we call the funny chicken dance … where they sort of throw up their wings and try to kick out with their feet at you because they want you to be away," she said.
"So other than not being able to fly, everything about that bird says that she's healthy and angry, which is just what we want."
Katherine McGrath of the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center says she and her colleagues have been 'delighted' by their voracious guest. (Submitted by Katherine McGrath)
Soon, McGrath says, the prodigious predator will fly free once more.

She's already losing weight and gaining mobility as staff feed her a restricted, all-natural diet, and take her for regular exercise in their enclosure. McGrath suspects she'll be ready to leave in a few weeks.
Before they release her, McGrath says the centre's staff will get in touch with nearby residents to give them a heads up and ask them to keep their chickens enclosed for a while.
"We do try to mitigate the ability for them to get into trouble again," she said.
Interview produced by Livia Dyring

articles.title: Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US change course
articles.summary: Despite an ostensible deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to bring diesel to the US, tankers are reportedly unable to dock due to existing sanctions.

image.caption: In October, Trump said 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel would be released to global marketsImage: Yoruk Isik/REUTERS

blocks.text: Several sanctioned tankers headed for the US carrying Russian diesel are said to have changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to data from marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com.
The tankers reportedly departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month and had declared their destinations as the US east coast.

This all comes after US President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil last month, in a deal with with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to secure a large amount of diesel directly to the US at a time when diesel prices have skyrocketed across the country.
The agreement caused shock and drew criticism in Ukraine and Europe. But it also was a logistical challenge, given that sanctions against Russia still remain in place.
It was also widely reported at the time that the amount of diesel in question was a fraction of the US daily demand.
Russia says reports are 'fake'
UK newspaper The Financial Times (FT) reported Wednesday that two of the tankers appeared to have changed their destination and were no longer headed to the United States.
Russian envoy and negotiator Kirill Dmitriev said on Thursday that the US-bound diesel tankers were still on course.
"Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev said on X, linking to the FT story.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said detail of shipments were a "commercial" matter that could not be made public.
"All diesel will find its buyers," he added, without elaborating.
A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the US but changed its destination from New York to a vague "for orders," without listing an unloading point.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
NJ governor threatens 'harsh penalties'

Despite the fact that the US Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill warned port and terminal operators to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
In a letter earlier this week, she warned that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill accused the Trump administration of lacking authority in overriding the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago.
She said New Jersey would act to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.
In a letter dated October 27, Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal warned shipping companies against violating US sanctions forbidding imports of Russian fuel.
"No president can unilaterally override a statute. Trump's license will not absolve you of legal and moral accountability," the letter read.

articles.title: Calgary friends win $90M in country's largest-ever lotto jackpot
articles.summary: A group of four Calgary friends who won the country’s largest-ever lottery jackpot had made their intentions clear with the name of their group chat: Manifesting Millions.

image.caption: From left to right: Hazeline Ong, Velna Ramirez, Lovelyn Malvar and Eidelson Elchico are splitting $90 million as the largest lottery winners in Canadian history. (Terri Trembath/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A group of four Calgary friends who won the country’s largest-ever lottery jackpot had made their intentions clear with the name of their group chat: Manifesting Millions.
Group of 4 won Oct. 20 Lotto Max draw

“It's almost like this stuff writes itself. It’s unbelievable how this has come together for this group,” said Steve Lautischer with Alberta Gaming, Liquor & Cannabis on Friday as he introduced the winners.
Now, Eidelson Elchico, Lovelyn Malvar, Hazeline Ong and Velna Ramirez will split the $90-million prize from the Oct. 20 Lotto Max draw.
The foursome had met about five years ago through family, and only started playing the jackpot together last month. They’d chosen one of their lucky numbers; the rest were random.
Elchico’s wife was the one to give them the idea to start playing, and he was the first to discover they had won.
He’d woken up in the middle of the night for a glass of water when he decided to check his phone. Still groggy at 3 a.m., he initially could not believe how many zeros he was looking at.
When he realized the size of the jackpot, he started calling the others, who were incredulous at the news.
“I thought it was a scam and I saw the email and I’m like, 'You definitely got scammed,'” said Malvar.
For the winners, it still feels surreal. Ramirez said it could take months or even a year before it fully sinks in.
The winners said they initially kept news of their jackpot quiet, telling only spouses and close family members.
And they're still working.
“I need the distraction; it’s too much,” Malvar said with a laugh.

As for what they plan to do with the money, while there were jokes about jets and private islands, the group also wants to do some good with their winnings, including donating to the Alberta Children’s Hospital.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca
With files from Terri Trembath

articles.title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, arrested in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material
articles.summary:
Father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said

Thomas Markle, the father of
articles.byline: Richard Luscombe in Miami and agencies

blocks.text: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a senior care facility in Polk county early on Friday, and made a brief initial appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday afternoon, the Associated Press reported.

A 14-page federal criminal complaint says that agents seized approximately 78 items and alleges that Markle kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units that he rented for nearly two decades.
An affidavit filed with the ​complaint that led to the arrest stated that two of the images inside the units showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a nude underage girl.

The document, filed in federal court in California, said the recovered material included dozens of slides, photographs, film negatives and books containing the illegal material. It said the FBI was still reviewing the material.

The director of the FBI, Kash ​Patel, said: “Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his ⁠criminal actions. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero ⁠safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”
Patel thanked FBI agents in Los Angeles and Tampa, and authorities in Mexico, the Philippines, and Marshall Islands that he said were involved in the investigation.

Some details in the criminal complaint are redacted, such as the name of the federal agent who signed the complaint, who states that they are assigned to the violent crimes against children unit in the LA office of the FBI. The case is presented as United States of America v Thomas Wayne Markle.

“Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the central district of California, said in a statement released by the US department of justice.
“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Essayli told the Associated Press that there was no evidence of victims in the US, based on the seized material, but that the investigation was ongoing. He said his office was aware of public reporting that Markle might have dementia.
Markle is charged with one count of possession of child sexual abuse material, and faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.
Efforts by the AP to reach Markle’s court-appointed lawyer for comment were unsuccessful, the news agency said.

Meghan, the wife of Prince Harry, said last month that she was “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images was found at her father’s former home in the Philippines.
The duchess also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about her father was sent to police in London in 2018.

She had issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his Philippines residence. He was named as a person of interest in the case earlier this week.

According to the justice department statement, FBI agents interviewed a person last month who was aware that Markle was renting the two storage units in California after the bureau became aware of developments in the Philippines.
Markle rented the units since 2008, it said, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Photographs produced by the Daily Mail showed Thomas Markle Sr being taken away in a wheelchair, in handcuffs, wearing a black T-shirt and surrounded by agents wearing jackets marked “FBI”. The UK tabloid asked Markle if he was a pedophile and he replied: “No.” Markle did not answer when the newspaper asked if he had ever collected child sexual abuse material.
A spokesperson for the duchess did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Authorities in the Philippines, where Markle ⁠had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he ​possessed child sexual abuse ​images. British police last month said they ​would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that ​claims had not ‌been passed to ​other authorities when ​they were first received.
He has denied the accusations, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies”.

Markle is a retired television lighting and photography director and he did not attend the 2018 wedding of Harry and Meghan, amid acrimony and estrangement between father and daughter. Meghan has since said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.
The duke and duchess returned to live in Britain in the summer after six years in the US.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

items: In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

articles.title: Stephen Miller named by Trump as new White House chief of staff
articles.summary: Trump said he would be replacing Susie Wiles for the top advisory role. Miller is controversial figure, known as a key architect of the administration's hardline immigration policies.

image.caption: Steven Miller is a long-time member of Trump's inner circleImage: Aaron Schwartz/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald ‌Trump announced on ⁠Friday ⁠that his ​deputy chief of ​staff and architect of his administration's strict immigration policy, Stephen Miller, will become his new chief of staff.
Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who had been in the post since Trump's inauguration. With the nod, Miller becomes the top aide to the president.
Trump announced the move, saying Miller was "one of my most trusted advisors," adding that Wiles has done an outstanding job, and would be "moving over" to the "Trump political operation."
"He gets it" and is "very good politically. And he's a very good man. He'll do a great job, great manager," Trump said.
Wiles also commented on her exit from the White House, saying that her work there was "the honor of a lifetime."
The move comes after Trump's Republican Party lost control of the House and Senate after a midterm election rout at the hands of Democrats.
One of Trump's longest-serving aides
The 41-year-old is one of Trump's longest-serving advisers, having joined Trump's longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter.
Although his portfolio as deputy chief of staff was wide-ranging, Miller is most responsible for Trump's policies and rhetoric on immigration.
Miller's appointment is a signal that Trump intends to continue on with his hardline immigration policies, despite voters rejecting Republicans around the country.
Miller is known for taking controversial positions, and is one of the Trump administration's most vocal advocates, frequently making media appearances to defend extreme positions.
Miller a controversial figure

On immigration, his ideas have included calling for federal agents to make 3,000 arrests every day, while allowing the agency to target migrants who have lived in the US for decades. He is widely created with helping expand the remit of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

On foreign policy, Miller has defended extrajudicial strikes on boats in Caribbean Sea allegedly used by drugs smugglers, and defended the administration's military operation to snatch Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January.
In January 2026, Miller went on broadcaster CNN and claimed that the US had the right the seize Greenland, after Trump said controlling the Danish territory was a strategic necessity.

"We live in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time," Miller told CNN's host Jake Tapper.
Miller also has not held back on attacking the administration's opponents.
During the midterm campaign, Miller called Democrats "extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics" on social media.
He also promoted claims about election fraud in California and Alaska, which were not substantiated.

As Trump has lost control of both chambers of Congress, Miller has been credited with working in the background to create an obstructionist strategy for the White House to block Democratic legislation. Trump has taken to the strategy and has said, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto."
Democrats vow to 'fight' Miller's agenda

After Trump's announcement, New York Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who could become the next speaker of the House, posted on social media that Miller was a "dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," referring to the deaths of US citizens protesting ICE raids.
Senator Chuck Schumer issued a statement saying the Trump had "learned nothing" after the Republican's election drubbing.
"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration," said Schumer, who is positioned to become the next Senate majority leader in January.
"Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way," he said.
US actions in Venezuela reflect Trump's 'strength' rhetoric

articles.title: Ueno Bank scandal plunges Paraguay into political crisis
articles.summary: Suspected financial fraud, public money at risk and millions of customers affected: Paraguay is in serious crisis following the sudden collapse of Ueno Bank. President Santiago Pena is facing…

image.caption: Still in office: Paraguay's President Santiago Pena tendered his resignation on Thursday, but it was not acceptedImage: Eitan Abramovich/AFP

blocks.text: The Ueno Bank collapse is turning into one of the biggest financial and political scandals in the history of Paraguay. At issue are suspected banking irregularities, hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, and business ties between the bank and the country's president, Santiago Pena.

The crisis was triggered on November 3, when the Paraguayan central bank (BCP) initiated resolution procedures against Ueno after determining that it had breached minimum solvency requirements. The public prosecutor has since announced three investigations into suspected financial crimes. 27 individuals have already been formally charged.

Pressure on President Pena intensified. On November 5, he tendered his resignation, but the Paraguayan Congress did not accept it. Instead, the Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to impeach him. A joint session of both legislative chambers was called to consider the resignation, but the session was not quorate, so no decision could be taken. Pena remains in office for now, and the Senate has opened impeachment proceedings.

blocks.caption: Lawmakers in the Paraguayan Congress have voted to impeach their presidentImage: Cesar Olmedo/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is Ueno Bank, and what happened?

Ueno Bank is a Paraguayan digital bank belonging to the Grupo Vazquez, a big Paraguayan conglomerate. Launched in 2021, it expanded remarkably fast: It recently had around three million customers, almost half the population of Paraguay. At the same time, there were warnings that the bank might have extended excessive loans to companies associated with its owners.

On November 3, 2026, the Paraguayan Central Bank (BCP) intervened, having determined that the bank had breached minimum solvency requirements: It no longer had sufficient capital to provide security for risks it had incurred. Business operations were abruptly suspended, leaving millions of customers unable to access their accounts.

blocks.caption: Police officers had to guard branches of Ueno Bank against protesting customers who couldn't withdraw their moneyImage: Daniel Duarte/AFP

blocks.text: What caused the crisis?
Investigations are primarily focused on three potential problems.
First, Ueno Bank is believed to have extended credit to other companies from the same group, and these may have exceeded legal limits.
Some business dealings may also have served to conceal the lack of capital, and make the bank's financial situation appear better than it actually was.
There is also the question of why the Central Bank didn't intervene sooner, despite indications that there were problems.
How much public money is managed by Ueno Bank?

Ueno Bank held huge deposits of public money. Its most important investors include the Instituto de Prevision Social (IPS), the Paraguayan social security agency responsible for pensions and social welfare payments. According to media reports, Ueno Bank administers public funds totalling as much as 800 to 850 million US dollars.

Not only is the size of the amount problematic, so is the concentration of public funds in a single financial institution — one that has had to be placed under state control. Other state institutions are also said to have continued to deposit funds with the bank.
This raises questions about how state institutions make their investment decisions, and the risks to which they have exposed public funds.
What are the bank's connections to Santiago Pena?

There is Pena's business relationship with Grupo Vazquez, to which the Ueno Bank belongs. The Paraguayan president maintained business connections with the conglomerate until March 2025, long after his election as head of state. However, he denies having had any direct involvement with the bank.

blocks.caption: In the Paraguayan Congress, a man holds up a sign calling for President Pena's impeachmentImage: Cesar Olmedo/REUTERS

blocks.text: On the other hand, Pena's appointment of Carlos Carvallo as president of the Central Bank in 2023 has come under scrutiny. The decision is controversial because until then Carvallo was the chair of the finance company that became Ueno Bank, Financiero Ueno. It raises questions about possible conflict of interest, and the independence of banking supervision.
Carvallo resigned on November 3, at Pena's request.
Who else is under suspicion?
On November 4, the public prosecutor's office formally charged 27 people: eight Ueno Bank executives, and 19 others with connections to companies associated with the bank.
The investigations are looking into suspected breach of trust, attempted fraud, breach of duty in crisis situations, and violation of the legal obligation to keep records.

On November 5, a judge remanded several former bank executives in custody, including Federico Miguel Vazquez Villasanti, the president of Grupo Vazquez. Two other accused were placed under house arrest.
What will happen now?

The Central Bank has initiated winding-up proceedings against Ueno Bank. Deposits of sums up to the equivalent of 37,600 US dollars per customer are protected by law. A law has also been passed that will enable around 20,000 US dollars per saver to be paid out early. However, it is still not clear when the affected customers will actually get their money back, or what will happen to deposits greater than the legally protected maximum.

blocks.caption: Paraguayans protest outside the Congress building in the capital, Asuncion. Around half the population is directly affectedImage: Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The political situation is more complicated. Santiago Pena tendered his resignation, but remains in office. A joint session of the two chambers of Congress could not decide whether or not to accept his resignation as the meeting was not quorate. The Senate has now initiated impeachment proceedings on charges of serious breaches of duty. Pena has announced that he will face the proceedings and exercise his right to defend himself.

What is at stake here is political immunity. If Pena leaves office in a regular way – by resigning — he will automatically become a senator for life, and this will give him parliamentary immunity from prosecution. If he is impeached, he loses this status, and can be prosecuted.

Should Pena leave office, the constitution decrees that his vice-president, Pedro Alliana, would take over as president. Congress would then have to elect a new vice-president. The current term of office runs until August 2028.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Tesla will stop making Cybertrucks next year: Musk
articles.summary: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival…

image.caption: New Tesla Cybertrucks are seen at SpaceX's Starship facility in Starbase, Texas, on Oct. 13. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.
Shift comes after years of weak sales

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk's pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker's autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.
Furthermore, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion US in combined market capitalization for the week.
A Tesla Cybertruck near the White House last year. (Leah Millis/Reuters)

While it wasn't immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialized components for the heavy, angular model.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."
Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

items: Elon Musk gets little bang for his buck in U.S. midterms, with possible Democratic investigations to come

blocks.text: The U.S. EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."
"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."
Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.
Tesla unveils electric Cybertruck, smashes its 'bulletproof' glass
'Cybertruck won't go, can't go'

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.
The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.
During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.
Elon Musk shows off redesigned Tesla Roadster that can thrust itself into the air
Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the U.S. market.
"All of them lost the competition because electric pickups aren't popular in the U.S.," Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged, stainless steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe, where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.
"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

articles.title: Morgan Fairchild, the icy diva you couldn't miss on 1980s TV, joins racy subscriber platform OnlyFans
articles.summary: Septuagenarian actress Morgan Fairchild is vowing to share another side of herself as the latest veteran soap opera vixen to join the racy online subscription platform OnlyFans.

image.caption: Morgan Fairchild, seen attending a movie premiere in 2003, is the latest 1980s soap vixen to join the online subscriber platform OnlyFans, saying she aims to show off a goofier, silly side. (Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Septuagenarian actress Morgan Fairchild is vowing to share another side of herself as the latest veteran soap opera vixen to join the racy online subscription platform OnlyFans.
Growing wave of veteran stars joining for-pay platform
Perhaps you remember the icy glam of her primetime TV roles or her scene-stealing turn as Chander Bing's spicy novelist mom on Friends.
But Morgan Fairchild is vowing to share another side of herself as the latest veteran soap vixen to join the racy online subscription platform OnlyFans.
"I'm putting up new pictures and videos. And before anyone asks: no, not that kind," the 76-year-old actress told U.S. media outlets, including People, TMZ and USA Today.
"Mostly, it's just me being goofy and talking about whatever's on my mind."

From left, actresses Linda Gray, Fairchild, Donna Mills, Loni Anderson and Nicollette Sheridan attend a Beverly Hills, Calif., event in 2023. Mills, who starred on Knots Landing, joined Onlyfans in July. (Randy Shropshire/Getty Images for Lifetime / A+E)

A mainstay on TV and in movies in the 1980s and '90s, Fairchild's wide-ranging credits run the gamut from soaps like Falcon Crest, Dallas and General Hospital to her regular cameo spots in episodes of hit shows like Mork & Mindy, Magnum, P.I., The Love Boat, Saturday Night Live, Murphy Brown and Friends.

"People know the characters, the clothes and the big hair... They may not know what a science nerd I am or how easily my sister can make me laugh. I'd love to share more of that," said the Dallas-born actress, who currently hosts the podcast 2 Bitches From Texas with her sister Cathryn Hartt.

She follows in the footsteps of friend and Knots Landing star Donna Mills, who joined OnlyFans this past July and has spoken positively in interviews about her experience thus far. Last spring, Mills went viral on social media with a post clapping back at an age-shaming comment she received.

items: Marmots on OnlyFans: Researchers turn to the internet for funding
How an Olympic medallist is using OnlyFans for additional income and independence
Olympians are turning to OnlyFans to fund dreams as they face a 'broken' finance system

blocks.text: An online platform where subscribers pay creators for custom photos and videos, OnlyFans is best known for its adult content and as a safer space for sex workers to make a living. It's been singled out amid wider debates about combatting sex trafficking and the exploitation of minors, with the platform announcing a ban of sexually explicit content in 2021, but backtracking days later.

More recently, however, a wider range of people looking to bolster their finances have joined the service, including a growing wave of famous faces aiming to connect with paying fans through tamer, non-explicit content.

American Pie's Shannon Elizabeth, Battlestar Galactica's Tricia Helfer, Drea de Matteo from The Sopranos and multiple stars from Baywatch are among the 1990s and early-2000s Hollywood stars who've signed up.
Elite athletes — including a raft of Olympians — have also turned to the platform as a source of income and financial stability while they navigate the steep costs of a competitive athletic career.

In recent years, more famous faces have joined Onlyfans, including, from left, Tricia Helfer from Battlestar Galactica, Shannon Elizabeth from American Pie and Baywatch's Erika Eleniak. (Unique Nicole /AFP/Getty, Kevin Winter/Getty, Alex J. Berliner/ABImages/Paramount Pictures/Getty)

articles.title: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
articles.summary:
The Chilean film-maker, whose films starred Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore and Rachel Weisz, died at his home in Santiago

Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of…

blocks.text: Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.

His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.

Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.

His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.

Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.

“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”

He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.

Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.

“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”
His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.
“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

articles.title: Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women
articles.summary:
Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing

Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward with at…

blocks.text: Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward with at least 10 more women suspected of being attacked by the disgraced star.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.
The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.
The Guardian also understands that next week the Met team that built the case against him will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.

The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.
Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.

The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.

Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating. I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”

Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases. Let’s see where this one goes.”
The trial, which spanned claims of attacks from 1999 to 2009, saw women asked by the defence barrister why they had not screamed during attacks.

Since the end of the trial there has been a debate about rape myths. A No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed calls from the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, for a legal duty that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions, should be examined.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.
“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths … we will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”
Siobhan Blake, the CPS lead for rape and serious sexual offences, said: “The focus must be the actions of the perpetrator and not the behaviour of the victim.

“We know that there is no typical response to sexual assault and myths that victims should scream and fight back are outdated. Some people may freeze or feel unable to speak about it for months or even years, but this is not a barrier to justice.”
Brand now faces years more of imprisonment and the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.

He was convicted on Thursday of raping a young fan at his luxury London townhouse in 2009, continuing despite her pleas for him to stop. He had picked her out of a crowd. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar.
Victims are expected to tell of the impact his crimes had on them in court on Monday.

Brand became an international star, acting in Hollywood films, and in latter years an online influencer, but was dogged by whispers and allegations about his danger to women. He was accused of treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.
The government says it is committed to reducing violence against women and girls by half.

Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.
“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to come forward.”

Later on the BBC, Burnham was asked about a statement of support for Brand in 2014 as the star faced media criticism, and said: “Well, over a decade ago, and all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do. His crimes are horrific.”

The comedian Katherine Ryan, who warned of a “predator” in the entertainment industry before Brand’s trial, said she felt relief at his conviction. “They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them,” she said.
“I will never be someone who, like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”

Bear Grylls, who baptised Brand when he converted to Christianity in 2024, said the star’s faith seemed genuine and added:“It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”
Brand was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” from charming to nasty as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.

articles.title: Critics say Democrats should look into Trump's Middle East deals in future corruption investigations
articles.summary: After their victory in the US midterm elections, the Democrats have promised to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Critics say the president's Middle East deals is an area they…

image.caption: During his second presidency, Donald Trump's first foreign trip was to visit dynastic rulers in the Middle East, who, he says, treated him like royaltyImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Several polls of US voters taken around the recent midterm elections show that an overriding concern about the Trump administration is corruption.
Just days after the midterms, senior figures in the Democratic Party were quick to proclaim that they will be investigating corruption accusations when they take their seats in January.
It's highly likely that many of those investigations will center on the Trump administration's and the Trump family's links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.

"The incoming Democratic majority in Congress will no doubt aggressively use their powers to investigate the administration's alleged wrongdoings," Amy Hawthorne, a non-resident fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Arab Center, wrote in a commentary after the midterms. "Cases involving the Middle East will be their top targets."

Financial disclosures made by President Trump in the middle of this year showed that during 2025, his businesses made about $2 billion in income. This was triple the income he reported the previous year, observers noted.

"According to the information available … Middle Eastern countries and businesses have directly contributed to the bottom line of Trump's family businesses — more so than any other region of the world," Brian Katulis, a senior fellow and expert in US foreign policy at the Middle East Institute in Washington, wrote in a July text after the presidential disclosure. "Gulf entities paid around $300 million to the president's businesses in 2025."
Billions in cryptocurrency
A lot of the money Trump made in 2025 came from the sale of a stake in a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, Katulis noted.

The company was founded by the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024 — Steve Witkoff is Trump's special envoy to the Middle East — and in 2025, a large portion of it was sold to an investment firm backed by a senior United Arab Emirates official, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The latter serves as the UAE's national security advisor and is also the brother of the UAE's president.

The deal was done in January 2026 behind closed doors, shortly before Trump's inauguration as president. In May 2026, the US agreed to allow the UAE access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, despite objections from some national security advisers.
Trump's critics allege a connection, the Trump administration denies it.

blocks.caption: Trump cryptocurrency: A law suit filed in late October alleges a UAE investment fund chaired by Tahnoon also spent about $2 billion on a World Liberty cryptocurrency to inflate the value of the company Image: Niklas Larsson/BILDBYRÅN/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are also other alleged instances of Trump administration corruption with links to the Middle East.
Trump Towers in the Middle East
Various Trump deals with Saudi and Emirati real estate developers are also being questioned because of possible conflicts of interest.

The Gulf real estate developers, which have close ties to their governments and respective royal families, have agreed to build Trump-branded golf resorts, hotels, mansions, skyscrapers and towers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and the Maldives.

In 2025, Trump reported $59.5 million in foreign real estate licensing income, ten times more than he made in 2023, business media outlet CNBC reported in August. Nearly two-thirds of that money came from projects in the Gulf, CNBC said.

Ethics watchdogs argue that, "the deals create conflicts between Trump's political leadership role and private interests" because some of those Gulf states and their developers were also "pursuing major US investments, seeking government permits or pressing for favorable economic and diplomatic relations."
Qatar's flying gift

When the Qatari royal family gifted Trump a luxury jet, worth around $400 million, in May 2025, politicians and ethics experts asked about the propriety of taking such a pricey present from a foreign government.

After his presidency ends, Trump was apparently planning to donate the plane to his Florida-based project, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation. Currently, it is unclear whether the Qatari plane will end up there and there's been speculation Trump will try to keep it for personal use.

blocks.caption: The luxury plane, described as a "flying palace," had to be retrofitted with additional security for an unspecified cost that's thought to be in the millions Image: Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS

blocks.text: The library is a non-profit and has received tens of millions in funding — an investigation by the CBS network traced over $100 million in donations — from lawsuits and via corporate donors.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already said the library project would be investigated. "Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," she told CBS.
Gaza's 'Board of Peace'
Plans for the so-called Board of Peace were created in September 2025 and the body was to facilitate a ceasefire and reconstruction in Gaza.

It was set up to be a kind of multilateral international organization, similar to the United Nations, except that Trump would serve as its chairman indefinitely and member countries donating $1 billion if they want to sit on the board permanently.
The Board of Peace has not achieved much in Gaza, experts say, and there have been several worrying developments.

Four months after its establishment, the World Bank account set up to manage Board of Peace funds was empty, the Financial Times newspaper reported in May. Instead, money had been deposited into a private JP Morgan bank account, over which there was no oversight.
There have apparently been contributions of around $3 million from Morocco and $20 million from the UAE, as well as pledges of $7 billion from board members and $10 billion from Trump.

The board's legal status was also changed to make it into an international non-governmental organization. This change in legal status may aim "to avoid US congressional oversight and keep much of its activity opaque," Zaha Hassan, an attorney and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warned in a June commentary. It also "gives Trump ultimate decision-making authority, including over financial matters," she noted.
'Trump crime family'
"The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities," the most senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, said after the midterms.
And he has already expressed concerns about the behavior of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in the Middle East.

Most of the issues around Kushner involve potential conflicts of interest. Kushner is acting as a volunteer envoy in the Middle East and has been deeply involved in negotiations to end the Gaza conflict and the Iran war.

blocks.caption: Kushner (right) next to Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Steve Witkoff (left): Kushner's status as a 'volunteer' envoy means he is not subject to the same scrutiny as an elected officialImage: Chen Junqing/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: In early October, CNN published an investigation that detailed links between Kushner's private equity company, Affinity Partners, and investments into leading Israeli military manufacturers.
It's also been reported that while he was travelling in the region, Kushner was trying to raise billions for his equity firm.

In March, Democratic politicians, including Garcia, wrote letters to the president's office, saying they had "serious concerns about whether the White House is letting Mr. Kushner use his influence for personal financial gain."
The potentially most damaging claims against Kushner come from a recent book, "Prince and Thieves," published late October by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole.

Cole alleges, "Kushner worked with the UAE to shape US policy across the Middle East and that, in the course of this work, he was given access to bank accounts containing roughly $2 billion," the New York Times wrote in its review.
Kushner denies the allegations about any such slush fund held by an Israeli bank and has threatened to sue Vanity Fair magazine, which published excerpts from the book.
But, as the New York Times concluded, "Cole's work is sufficiently calm, detailed and forensic to necessitate a large-scale and urgent congressional inquiry."
