articles.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’
articles.summary:
The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds

As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch…

blocks.text: As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.

Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.

The colour of noise tends to animate physicists more than linguists, but researchers at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US found the concept provided fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.

Kathryn O’Nell, the first author on the study, said: “In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.
“It’s particularly cool for conversation, because you can stay somewhere long enough to really get to know each other, to understand the topic, but you’re not stuck there while it gets stale.”

The researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, who answered questions on the chats afterwards. People enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise, they found.

To see whether the effect applied beyond strangers, the researchers ran a similar analysis on conversations between friends about their formative experiences. Again, more pink noise meant more enjoyment.

The effect had real-world consequences, too. When the scientists turned to speed-dating conversations, they found that more pink noise predicted which pairs met up for a second date. Details have been published in Science Advances.

blocks.caption: Cicero had plenty of conversational pointers. Over 2,000 years later, scientists are still exploring the secrets of a successful chinwag. Photograph: Jozef Sedmak/Alamy

blocks.text: Nailing down what makes a great chat is notoriously tricky, the researchers said. In a bold opening statement to their paper, the authors write: “Good conversation is like pornography – it is difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.”

Colloquially, people talk about being in sync, but the metaphor misses something, said Dr Emily Finn, a neuroscientist and senior author on the paper. “In sync can be incredibly dull,” she said. People can be in sync when they repeat each other’s words and circle a single subject. They might well be immensely bored.

In the study, the scientists took conversations and fed each side into an AI called MPNet. The program scored every turn of the chat on 768 different criteria, covering aspects such as meaning, tone and context. This allowed the scientists to quantify how conversations ebbed and flowed over time.

Conversations exhibit white noise when people fail to follow what has just been said: the chat might jump all over the place, or be dominated by a person who seems oblivious to the other person’s responses. Other conversations can have red noise, which arises when people mirror each other’s language and fall into a conversational rut.

Pink noise lies somewhere in between: a conversational Goldilocks zone that balances stability and flexibility. People will synchronise as they explore a topic, then drift apart as they pull in fresh ideas before converging again to explore those.

The pinkiness of a conversation depends on the people involved, but O’Nell said she suspected the skill could be learned and developed. As part of the study, the team analysed podcasts fronted by two hosts and found that the pinkiness of their conversations increased over the first 50 episodes.

Prof Elizabeth Stokoe, a conversation analyst at the London School of Economics, praised the researchers for moving beyond the idea that “more similarity is better”. But asking whether a conversation is enjoyable risks missing the point, she added.

“There’s a lovely study of a phone call in which a father and his daughter, a young woman with learning disabilities living in residential care, take a long time to say goodbye, and the ending is painful and poignant,” she said. “Reducing conversations to whether they are ‘enjoyable’ can feel bloodless, since many of the conversations that matter most in our lives are like this.”

articles.title: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
articles.summary:
Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom

Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as…

blocks.text: Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.

Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

“The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used,” the police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster. “An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacenter is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”
after newsletter promotion

A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.

“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.

Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.

But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

articles.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
articles.summary: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide…

image.caption: Ilse Aigner is the speaker of Bavaria's parliament, and reportedly the front-runner for a joint Christian Democrat nomination to be the next German president [FILE: October 24, 2026]Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU, want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.
It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel, the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.
DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.
On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

blocks.caption: Aigner appears to have the backing of both Bavaria's Markus Söder and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, visible in the background on the main stage at the CSU party conference in this photoImage: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's first woman as president?

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.
She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.
Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.
Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.
She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

blocks.caption: Aigner is the speaker or president of Bavaria's state parliament at present, she's also a former federal agriculture minister Image: Rolf Poss/IMAGO

blocks.text: What steps remain on the path to Germany picking a new president?
The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.
A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.
It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.
Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.
The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.
This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

articles.title: Ontario council seat decided by a draw out of a wedding hat from 1883, after tied vote
articles.summary: After a long campaign, a recount and two weeks of uncertainty, the race for a Norfolk County council seat was left up to fate. Chris Van Paassen will return as Ward 4 councillor after Norfolk County…

image.caption: Jeni Lambert, left, stands beside returning Norfolk County Ward 4 councillor Chris Van Paassen on Nov. 5 in Simcoe, Ont. Van Paassen's name was drawn out of a hat, securing his victory after a tied vote in the Oct. 26 municipal election. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton

After a long campaign, a recount and two weeks of uncertainty, the race for a Norfolk County council seat was left up to fate. Chris Van Paassen will return as Ward 4 councillor after Norfolk County Clerk William Tigert drew his name from a hat Thursday night, breaking a tie with challenger Jeni Lambert.
Chris Van Paassen returns to council for Ward 4 after he and challenger Jeni Lambert each received 858 votes
After a long campaign, a recount and two weeks of uncertainty, one Norfolk County council seat was left up to fate.
Chris Van Paassen will return as Ward 4 councillor after Norfolk county clerk William Tigert drew his name from a black top hat from 1883 Thursday night, breaking a tie with challenger Jeni Lambert.

Both candidates received exactly 858 votes in the Oct. 26 municipal election. A recount Thursday morning confirmed those numbers were accurate, leaving the county with an unusual problem: two candidates, one council seat and no clear winner.

items: Full 2026 election results for Burlington, Brantford, Norfolk County and Haldimand County

blocks.text: "I've been involved in municipal elections for 35 years and this is the first tie vote that I've experienced," Tigert said.
He says under the Municipal Elections Act, it says if there's a tie vote after the recount, then the clerk is required to draw the name by lot for the successful candidate.
Top hat used in draw came from county archives

Enter the hat, which was selected by county archivist Joshua Klar. In an email to CBC Hamilton, Klar said it belonged to Samuel Sowden, a farmer and businessman from Woodhouse Township, who wore it at his wedding in February 1883.
He says the hat is believed to have been purchased at a local shop in Simcoe.
"I selected this particular top hat since it was in excellent condition," he said.
Tigert, the clerk, said the county may add a note to the archives about the hat's role in this election.
Incumbent said the process was stressful for the community
At 7 p.m., two cards featuring the names of candidates were placed inside the hat. Tigert then drew one name.
"I was only prepared for having Jeni's name pulled," Van Paassen said afterward. "I was not prepared for having my name pulled."
The incumbent said he was relieved to finally have an answer after weeks of uncertainty, but acknowledged that waiting for the result was stressful for the community.
He also credited Lambert for running a strong campaign, saying that the tied vote showed her message resonated.
For Lambert, the result was disappointing, but she said she was proud of the campaign she ran and had no regrets.
"I'm a very community-oriented person and I will continue to be very community-oriented," she said. "I just won't have a seat around the official table to do so."
Candidate would prefer a more democratic way of settling a tie
Lambert said she would like to see the legislation changed to allow for a more democratic way of settling a tied result, such as another head-to-head vote between the candidates.
"Having something as important as this left up to chance, I'm worried is going to push people away even more," she said.

items: The fate of a tied council race for Norfolk County’s Ward 4 may be left up to chance

blocks.text: While the draw has produced a winner, Van Paassen's return to council isn't technically official just yet.

The legislation allows 15 days for someone involved in the recount to apply for a judicial recount. If no application is filed, Tigert can officially declare Van Paassen elected on the 16th day after Thursday's recount.
Tigert said no ballots were contested during the recount.
Every vote matters, both candidates say
Both candidates also used the experience to make a point about voter participation.
Norfolk County reported turnout of 33 per cent in the Oct. 26 election, with 20,162 ballots cast among 61,085 eligible voters.
Lambert said the tie is a reminder that even one additional vote could have changed the outcome.
"When they say every vote matters, this is the perfect example that it really does," she said.
Jeni Lambert, left, and Chris Van Paassen. The two candidates running to be Norfolk County’s Ward 4 councillor were tied at 858 votes. (Submitted)
Van Paassen, who was first elected in 1994, echoed that message, saying municipal government has a direct impact on residents' everyday lives.
He hopes to see turnout climb to between 60 and 90 per cent in future municipal elections.
For now, he says he hopes to work with Lambert despite the unusual way the race ended.
"Thank you very much to all the residents of Ward 4 and the support from across Norfolk County," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeffery is a reporter with CBC Hamilton. He previously worked as a reporter at CBC Saskatchewan in Regina, and was an associate producer at CBC Toronto. You can reach him at jeffery.tram@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Meghan Markle's father arrested in US over child sex abuse material
articles.summary: US federal agents arrested Thomas Markle in Florida. The Duchess of Sussex and television actress Meghan Markle, who is estranged from her father, said she was "deeply distressed" by the charges.

image.caption: Thomas Markle Sr. is set to appear in a Florida district court Image: Chris Urso/REUTERS

blocks.text: Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle Sr., was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child abuse, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls,US federal prosecutors said.
Thomas Markle Sr. was charged with one count of possession of child sex abuse imagery, prosecutors said in a statement.
The 82-year-old was arrested outside the city of Tampa on Florida's west coast.
The director of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Kash Patel, said that "Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."
Patel said their agents "moved quickly" to identify and locate the explicit material, and then arrested Markle Sr. in Florida.
Sex abuse images discovered in storage units

First Assistant US Attorney for central California Bill Essayli said federal agents searched two storage units in the Los Angeles area and "seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books" that contained suspected child sexual abuse images.

"Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," said Essayli in a statement. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law."
If convicted, Thomas Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

Markle Sr. was first reported to the police in the Philippines and to the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jr, after he claimed to have found child sex abuse material at his father's home in the Philippines, according to reports by the UK newspaper The Sun.
Meghan Markle, the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's home.
She revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
The FBI said last month that it would assist Philippine authorities with the case where possible.

blocks.caption: Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said last month she was deeply troubled by allegations surrounding her entranged father. [FILE: 2021]Image: Photoshot/Avalon/picture alliance

blocks.text: Meghan's father famously didn't attend her wedding at Windsor Castle
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the US television drama "Suits," married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018.
Her father did not attend their wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.
Thomas Markle Sr., a retried television lighting and photography director, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated.
That forced him to return to the US.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him."

articles.title: Joly asks Competition Bureau to investigate Cleveland-Cliffs purchase of Stelco
articles.summary: Canada's industry minister is asking the Competition Bureau to investigate Stelco's parent company after its CEO told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his…

image.caption: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she is calling for the investigation after what she called the CEO's 'confessions' about the purchase of Stelco. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's industry minister is asking the Competition Bureau to investigate Stelco's parent company after its CEO told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his U.S. business.
CEO said he bought Hamilton plant to stop it undercutting U.S. company
Mélanie Joly said on Friday she has sent a letter to the competition commissioner asking them to examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs's conduct ran afoul of the Competition Act.
"If negotiations and acquisition were conducted in bad faith, Canadians deserve to know. The company needs to face the consequences," she said in a statement.

Last week, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC's Power & Politics with David Cochrane "I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company."
Stelco owner's live TV admission prompts industry minister to call lawyers
Joly called that a "shocking admission" and said she contacted the department's lawyers to see if there should be any consequences.
"It is the commissioner's responsibility to examine this matter thoroughly and, if warranted, take the appropriate measures," she said on Friday.
Goncalves made his comments after Joly's demand that the company reverse its layoffs at Stelco or face potential legal action.

Stelco owner says he could sell plant next year

blocks.text: The government says the company agreed when it purchased Stelco to keep the number of unionized employees at 2024 levels through to 2029.
Goncalves's company maintains that it's in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act.

articles.title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over confrontation with journalist
articles.summary:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has…

blocks.text: Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after the former comedian had been found guilty of rape.
Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”
Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”
“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching.
In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.

He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.
“I have made such a report.”

The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.
Brand had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.
After the trial, experts added to calls for a change in the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”.
In his closing speech, Winter said none of the complainants had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” during their encounters with Brand.

Claire Waxman, who is the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, is seeking to update the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”. She criticised “outdated and harmful assumptions” that victims must have screamed or tried to fight off their attacker.

The head of Scotland Yard, Mark Rowley, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he supported Waxman’s call. “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards, it’s getting very close to victim-blaming, which is something we’ve thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don’t do.

“People fall into myths about [how] a rape victim must behave in a certain way, must react in a certain way. The evidence is really clear. Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.” On Friday a No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, agreed with Waxman’s position.

Speaking after the trial Urwin told a Times podcast she approached Winter after the verdict because her name had been mentioned during the trial. “I thought he’s talked about me a lot, I’ll go and introduce myself and that is a legitimate thing to do,” she said. “I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way.”

It is understood that several complaints have been submitted to the Bar Standards Board but the regulator said it would not “comment as to whether or not it has received any information about potential misconduct by a barrister regardless of how any information comes to our attention”.
A spokesperson said complaints were usually handled confidentially unless they resulted in a disciplinary tribunal hearing.
The comedian Katherine Ryan criticised the barrister on her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, saying: “That was so unprofessional, so inappropriate, so aggressive. Really sickening.”

Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way. There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.

“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.
“By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.
“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury … who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”

blocks.caption: The jury found Russell Brand guilty of rape. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by the Times, the Sunday Times and a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for his client to have a fair trial.
The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.

In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had accused the journalists who first exposed him as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.
But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths but we are going further by changing the law to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations being weaponised against rape victims. We will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”
Brand, 51, was convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009 and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009.
He is in custody and due to be sentenced on Monday.

articles.title: Iran war: Gulf tanker attacked, 1 seaferer killed
articles.summary: Iran is stepping up attacks on shipping in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. A Greek-owned tanker believed to have been struck with a missile, and Iran said two other vessels were on fire.

image.caption: UK Maritime Trade Operations Center said at least five ships have been attacked in the Gulf.Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: An explosion believed to have been caused by a missile attack on ‌an oil ⁠tanker in the Persian Gulf left one seafarer dead, the vessel's operating company said on Friday.
Greek management firm Velos Tankers said the ​Marshall Islands-flagged tanker MT Velos Sapphire ​was sailing towards Bahrain when it ‌was attacked.

"The company is ‌greatly saddened to report the ‌death ​of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been ​reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the firm said.
The explosion caused a fire to break out in the ship. The crew were able to extinguish the fire without reporting any other injured.
Bahrain's Khalifa Bin Salman Port ultimately took in the ship and now a investigation into the incident will be launched to assess the extent of the damage to the vessel's hull.
Shipping crews caught in the crossfire of the Hormuz conflict
Iran using 'everything it can' to stop oil flows
The incident is the latest in a string of attacks on ships in the Persian Gulf by Iran.

US newspaper The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) cited regional officials, security firms and analysts in a report detailing how Iran is using everything it can to stop the flow of oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the report, Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships over recent weeks.
According to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center (UKMTO), October saw the highest monthly number of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, with more than 35 incidents.
At least five vessels have been attacked so far in November, UKMTO added.

The increasing attacks coincides with signs of recovery in shipping through Hormuz. US Central Command said last month it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.
On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers were on fire in the strait, state media reported.
Iran destroys missile over Qeshm island
Meanwhile, Iranian media said ​on Friday ​that Iranian ​air defenses ‌had destroyed a US ‌MQ-1 drone ‌over Qeshm Island in the Strait ​of Hormuz.
The ‌United States did not confirm the incident.
It all comes in the wake of the US launching strikes on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, with Iranian state media reporting five explosions in rapid succession.
A statement attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that the Middle East war would widen if the US resumes its attacks.
Khamenei has rejected the notion that Washington will change course after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.summary: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.

blocks.text: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.

Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.

The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

articles.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
articles.summary: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and…

image.caption: Travellers are seen at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague on Friday after Czech police registered bomb threats against flights arriving and departing from the airport, amid a series of similar threats affecting flights across Europe. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

blocks.text: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations to conduct security sweeps.

No explosives have been found, and the threats have so far proved unfounded. But the spate of hoaxes that affected a number of flights, airports and, as of Friday, news broadcasters has raised concern over the widening impact if the threats continue to spread.

It's not yet clear if the incidents are linked, but the bomb threat hoaxes come on the heels of other European disruptions, including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
Here is what we know about the hoaxes targeting airlines and broadcasters in Europe.
When did the threats begin?
What appeared to be a co-ordinated wave of bomb threats targeting European air traffic began on Tuesday.

At least seven flights and a cruise ship received hoax bomb threats, triggering emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and temporary airport closures in countries including Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain.
A second wave was reported on Thursday, with at least 27 flights affected.
Bomb threats force multiple flights in Europe to make emergency landings

On Friday, Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain.
How are newsrooms involved?

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov" claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.
The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

Garda members work outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE on Friday after staff were evacuated from the site following a bomb threat. The broadcaster has claimed the bomb threat is from the same group that has been behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)
How are the threats sent?

Bomb threats against planes are often communicated to airlines, airports or authorities through anonymous emails or phone calls claiming that an explosive device is on board. Authorities do not always disclose how threats are delivered, because doing so could encourage copycats and compromise investigations.

A Prague airport representative told CNN on Thursday that they had received a threat from an anonymous email addressed to the airport, and Czech police said similar emails went to other European airports.

Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, told Reuters that an airline's security department first runs the report through a checklist. It then alerts the authorities, who may scramble fighter jets or divert the plane to a designated airport for a full sweep.
What are the risks?
The vast majority of bomb threats turn out to be false alarms, though all must be treated as real until investigated, which means authorities are forced to scramble to rule out any danger.
No explosive device has been found on the planes affected this week, but every airline must decide whether a threat is credible and act accordingly.
A spokesperson for the British government called this week's incidents "malicious hoax threats" and said it has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world."

items: String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe
Bomb threats affect at least 27 flights, leading to emergency landings at several European airports

blocks.text: Airlines are not new to bomb threats, but aviation security experts say the apparent co-ordination and timing of the current incidents is unusual.
All planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.
Who is behind the threats?
Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government.

The incidents come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response.
Countries affected by the disruptions, including Denmark, Poland and ​Romania, have previously accused Moscow. Russia denies any involvement.
An EasyJet aircraft takes off at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State," a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia.
Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.
What is their goal?

Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said bomb threats can stem from a wide range of motives, including political grievances, activist campaigns, criminal activity, online groups or state-linked hybrid operations.

European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen says that since 2022, Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference.
“We are under attack all the time,” she told Reuters. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilize our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.”
“It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations. Quite often, it is Russia.”
How have airlines been affected?
Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority.

Even a false alarm can disrupt airlines' operations, with plane diversions and thorough security inspections causing delays for passengers. Carriers typically bear additional costs including fuel, passenger rebooking, crew disruption and aircraft diversions.
Schouten said a sweep means unloading passengers and baggage, searching the aircraft and reloading. That can push crews past duty limits and lead to missed connections and cancellations.
People gather outside the offices of Irish national broadcaster RTE as officials conduct a security sweep after a reported bomb threat on Friday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)
Air France-KLM chief executive Ben Smith said on Thursday he had never previously seen threats reported in such a co-ordinated fashion.

"We're quite confident that we have in place what we need to ensure that it has minimal or no impact on our operation," Smith told reporters. "So we have no ask today of our governments to change the way they manage these types of situations."
Which airlines, airports have been affected?

blocks.text: What measures are being taken?
Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice-president of the European Cockpit Association.
Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

articles.title: Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck
articles.summary: Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive…

image.caption: A Cybertruck might be parked at sites like Tesla's Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg, but the vast pickup is not road legal in Germany [FILE: April 23, 2026]Image: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

blocks.caption: Cybertrucks fit on LA's wide roads with relative ease, but that's not the case everywhereImage: Barry King/Alamy/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did the Cybertruck fail to attract customers?
Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."
For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."
However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.
Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.
Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.
Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

blocks.caption: The agressive set-square design appealed to some of the more eccentric and well-financed police departments in the US like casino capital Las VegasImage: Ty ONeil/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How far short of Musk's sales targets did the Cybertruck fall?
Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.
But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.
At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.
For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

blocks.caption: SpaceX purchased a vast fleet of Cybertrucks in 2025, perhaps feeling the futuristic styling fits the company's aesthetics, or perhaps as a favor to a friendImage: Charles Briggs/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the story with the next pet project, the Cybercab?
The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.
Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

blocks.caption: Tesla held a Cybercab launch party in Ausitin in September this yearImage: Bob Daemmrich/ZUMA/picture alliance

articles.title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
articles.summary: Jim Messina tells the BBC that after Democrats' midterm victories he's talked to "over two dozen campaigns", with some already hiring staff.

blocks.text: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.
"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.
He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.
He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"
Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.
"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.
"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."

Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".
"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.

items: PODCAST: Hear more from Jim Messina on Americast

blocks.text: Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.

"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.
Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".
The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

articles.title: Data center protesters break into Microsoft site in Amsterdam
articles.summary: Protesters are demanding a pause in data center construction in Europe. Campaigners planning protests in 16 countries say the AI building boom threatens water supplies, power grids and climate goals.

image.caption: The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operatingImage: Koen van Weel/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, climbing cranes and hanging balloons while police stood by.

The action opened two days of planned protests in 16 countries, with campaigners demanding a pause in major artificial intelligence data center construction over concerns about electricity, water and environmental damage.
What happened in Amsterdam?
More than 100 activists gathered at the site, marching arm in arm before entering. Some danced or carried placards reading: "Screw your data center."
"These data centers are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said.

blocks.caption: Image: Koen van Weel/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than $1 billion (€890 million) in the project, urged protesters to leave safely and discuss their concerns.
Microsoft said it respected people's right to express their views peacefully but did not condone unlawful actions.

The Stop Dirty Data Centres coalition said other planned actions included a march in Dublin, a protest outside Poland's parliament and a demonstration against another Microsoft data center in Denmark.
Why are campaigners opposing data centers?
The protest group said more demonstrations are planned in several European countries on Saturday, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the UK.
Campaigners say the facilities strain electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for resources and threaten climate goals.
They also raise concerns about job losses and the concentration of power in technology companies.
The coalition said it was not calling for existing data centers to close. It wants governments to establish clearer rules before further large-scale construction proceeds.
Technology companies argue that data centers provide essential infrastructure for AI and cloud services used by businesses, governments and consumers.

The dispute comes amid growing scrutiny of the industry's expansion. A Google project in Finland faces a criminal investigation over land clearances, while Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental rules for data centers.
The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operating.

articles.title: Despite Russia impasse, Germany still hoping to host Men's Ice Hockey World Championship
articles.summary: A week after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey, the way forward remains unclear. Berlin is seeking a solution that will allow Germany to host next year's…

image.caption: Skoda has long been the main sponsor of the Men's World Ice Hockey ChampionshipImage: Vit Simanek/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A German government spokesman has said that despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since last Friday's decision, several leading ice hockey nations, including Finland, Sweden and Czechia have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada late next month, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russian participation would render the hosting of the World Championship "practically impossible, both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

However, he also said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the World Championship – as planned – in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf next May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled. However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore—through dialogue—how we can still ensure the tournament takes place," he said.

Following last Friday's CAS decision ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as World Championship host.
German visa restrictions on Russians in place

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a German interior ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult due to restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy'—and we will certainly not pretend that there is," Martin Giese said.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."
Consensus remains elusive
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision – before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark – and with the clock ticking towards the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26,

articles.title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance
ByBernd Debusmann
White House reporter
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways.
The 2026 winners who now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

items: Dozens eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

blocks.text: Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is an oil spill and how does it affect communities?
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported an oil spill in Mariveles, Bataan, on Friday, affecting approximately 500 square meters of coastal waters.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 12:05am
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported an oil spill in Mariveles, Bataan, on Friday, affecting approximately 500 square meters of coastal waters.

In the Philippines, damage caused by oil spills reached P4.93 billion in 2023, accounting for 53% of the total damage from human-induced disasters recorded that year, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
What are oil spills and how does it affect us?

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) defines crude oil as a fossil fuel used to manufacture a wide array of petroleum products, ranging from transportation fuels like gasoline to materials such as asphalt, plastics, soaps, and paints.
NOAA noted that oil spills can occur on both small and large scales, with either posing significant threats to marine life.

“Most of these spills are small, for example, when oil spills while refueling a ship. But these spills can still cause damage, especially if they happen in sensitive environments, like beaches, mangroves, and wetlands,” the agency explained.
“Large oil spills are major, dangerous disasters. These tend to happen when pipelines break, big oil tanker ships sink, or drilling operations go wrong,” it added.

One of the Philippines' notable large-scale oil spills occurred in 2024, when the MT Terranova sank off the coast of Bataan while carrying 1.4 million liters of industrial fuel oil. During cleanup operations, the PCG reported recovering more than 1 million liters of oily waste.
Impacts
Oil spills threaten marine life as well as the livelihoods and safety of coastal communities near the affected waters.
The Department of Health (DOH) has warned against the health risks of exposure to oil spills, whether through inhalation, direct skin contact, or ingestion:

items: Through inhalation: Nausea, eye irritation, increased blood pressure, irregular heart rhythm, headache, loss of appetite, and difficulty concentrating;
Through skin contact: Skin irritation, blisters, burns, peeling skin, and dermatitis;
Through ingestion: Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, coughing, irritability, and unconsciousness. Large amounts may result in convulsions, coma, or death.

blocks.text: As safety precaution, the Health Department advised posting warning signs around affected areas and water bodies, exercising extra caution with drinking water, and keeping children away from the site, as their tendency to put their hands in their mouths puts them at higher risk of accidental ingestion.
The DOH advised individuals exposed to oil to immediately remove and decontaminate contaminated clothing and thoroughly wash affected skin with mild soap and water.
Meanwhile, the DOH urged anyone experiencing symptoms after exposure to an oil spill to seek immediate medical attention at the nearest healthcare facility. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: LTFRB extends regularization application period for 'tempo' TNVS by 30 days
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has extended the application deadline for the regularization of ride-hailing service providers operating under temporary or “tempo”…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 12:03am

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has extended the application deadline for the regularization of ride-hailing service providers operating under temporary or “tempo” status by another 30 days.
The LTFRB previously set a 30-working-day window for online applications, which began on October 8.

Acting upon the directive of Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon, the agency said the extension aims to ensure no one is left behind in the public transportation sector, particularly among Transport Network Vehicle Services (TNVS) operators.

“Our regularization move is aimed at helping thousands of TNVS drivers whose only fault was that they relied in good faith on their onboarding and assumed substantial financial commitments in the process,” LTFRB acting chairman Greg Pua Jr. said.

“Tempo” is known in the transport community, especially in TNVS, as a practice of the Transport Network Companies (TNCs) of onboarding TNVS units on their digital platforms without the units having obtained the requisite authority from the LTFRB.

The agency explained that operating under tempo status violates LTFRB rules and regulations, as it allows TNVS units to offer transport services to the commuting public despite lacking valid authorization.
Based on the latest agency data, the LTFRB has received 13,216 applications, of which 5,091 have already been granted provisional authority.
Pua said the agency is fast-tracking the processing of all applications. He urged applicants to upload all necessary documents to avoid processing delays.

“We ask our partners in the TNVS community who are applying for the regularization to follow the process of the application. The requirements are intended to prevent application cancellations due to some challenges that include questions on vehicle ownership,” Pua said.

Applications for regularization can be submitted through the LTFRB's online platform. Applicants having difficulty complying are advised to reach out to the agency to seek assistance.—Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News
